terminal.title: Democrats Debate Iran War Powers as Strikes Test Party Unity
terminal.description_short: After U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, Democrats disagreed over a war-powers resolution and Israel policy, creating a test of party unity ahead of 2026 primaries.
terminal.description_medium: An Associated Press report published March 2, 2026, said U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran tested Democratic unity. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called for a war-powers vote, while Reps. Greg Landsman and Josh Gottheimer opposed the measure and Sen. John Fetterman disputed claims that the attack was illegal. The report also described disagreement over Israel and AIPAC’s role in primaries.
terminal.description_long: The Associated Press reported on March 2, 2026, that U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran were testing a Democratic coalition that had largely opposed President Donald Trump’s immigration tactics and criticized his economic policies. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called for a war-powers resolution to constrain the president’s options. The article reported differences within the party: Reps. Greg Landsman and Josh Gottheimer said they would not support the measure, and Sen. John Fetterman rejected arguments that the attack was illegal. It also situated the dispute in a longer debate about Israel and Gaza. AIPAC’s affiliated super PAC had opposed Tom Malinowski after he questioned unconditional aid to Israel; in New Jersey’s special primary, progressive Analilia Mejia defeated him. In Illinois, mayor Daniel Biss criticized AIPAC-aligned groups ahead of another primary. The article presented these developments as a political test, not proof of a lasting party realignment.

supported_facts_and_quotes: The article says U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran 'could test the durability' of Democratic cohesion.
It reports that Chuck Schumer called for a war-powers resolution to restrain the president’s attack options.
It says Greg Landsman would not back an Iran resolution, Josh Gottheimer said he would vote no, and John Fetterman rejected arguments that the attack was illegal.
It reports that AIPAC’s affiliated super PAC opposed Tom Malinowski after he questioned unconditional aid to Israel, and that Analilia Mejia won New Jersey’s special primary.
It reports that Daniel Biss criticized AIPAC-aligned groups before an Illinois primary.
limitations: The report describes an emerging political test and competing positions; it does not establish a final war-powers vote result or a lasting party realignment.
It does not support the frozen synopsis’s claims of measurable institutional stress, public-trust erosion, or accountability pressure.

supported_facts_and_quotes: The Associated Press story says U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran 'could test the durability' of Democratic cohesion.
It reports Schumer’s call for a war-powers resolution and differences among Landsman, Gottheimer, and Fetterman over the measure and the attack’s legality.
It reports the AIPAC-affiliated super PAC’s opposition to Malinowski, Mejia’s New Jersey primary victory, and Biss’s criticism of AIPAC-aligned groups ahead of an Illinois primary.
limitations: This is an AP syndication of the same political report; it does not establish a vote result, measurable downstream harm, or a lasting party realignment.

terminal.title: Erik Prince Team Pitched White House on El Salvador Detention Camp Plan
terminal.description_short: Politico reported that Erik Prince’s team pitched a proposed El Salvador detention and deportation operation; no approval was established.
terminal.description_medium: Politico reported on April 11, 2025, that former Blackwater chief Erik Prince and defense contractors pitched the White House on a plan involving a 10,000-person detention camp in El Salvador and transportation for as many as 100,000 people. The article describes a proposal, not an approved contract or an operating program, and says White House interest was unclear.
terminal.description_long: On April 11, 2025, POLITICO reported that former Blackwater chief Erik Prince and defense contractors were pitching the White House on a proposal connected to deportations to El Salvador. The proposal described gathering as many as 100,000 people from U.S. prisons, holding them in a 10,000-person detention camp, and flying them to El Salvador. It said Prince’s group, partnering with El Salvador, would handle the logistics and would need access to government immigration files held by law-enforcement agencies to determine people’s immigration status. The proposal claimed a contract would help resolve legal issues and improve the government’s ability to locate, capture, detain, and deport immigrants; those were claims in the pitch, not legal findings. An administration official expected the proposal to be discussed during Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele’s planned White House visit. Prince and the White House declined to comment. POLITICO also reported that an LLC called 2USV was registered in Wyoming, which the article described as an indication that Prince’s group hoped to move to a more serious phase of pitching. The report describes proposed terms and a contractor pitch; it does not report an awarded contract or say the camp or flights began.

supported_facts: POLITICO reports that Erik Prince and defense contractors were pitching the White House on an operation connected to deportations to El Salvador.
The proposal described gathering ‘100,000 of the worst criminal offenders’ from U.S. prisons, holding them at a 10,000-person detention camp, and flying them to El Salvador.

The proposal said Prince’s group would work in partnership with El Salvador, handle logistics, and need access to government immigration files held by law-enforcement agencies to determine immigration status.

The proposal claimed a contract would help resolve legal issues and improve the government’s ability to locate, capture, detain, and deport immigrants; POLITICO attributes this claim to the proposal rather than a legal finding.
An administration official expected the pitch to be discussed during Nayib Bukele’s planned White House visit; Prince and the White House declined to comment.
POLITICO reports an LLC called 2USV was registered in Wyoming and characterizes it as an indication that the group hoped to move to a more serious phase of pitching.
limitations: The article reports proposed terms and a contractor pitch. It does not report an awarded contract or that the camp or flights began.
The proposal’s legal claims are not legal findings; the article does not establish a $100 million agreement, implementation, completed deportations, or a violation of law.

supported_facts: CNN’s April 9 report says the administration had fielded a pitch from Erik Prince for a U.S.-run immigrant detention facility in El Salvador.
CNN reports mixed views among officials about that detention-facility idea, with some seeing potential utility and others viewing it as legally tenuous and unrealistic.
limitations: This is separate earlier reporting and does not establish the April 11 POLITICO proposal’s 10,000-person camp, 100,000-person scale, or specific logistics.

terminal.title: Lawmakers Question Iran War’s Goals and Endgame as Trump Considers Winding Down Operations, AP Reports
terminal.description_short: AP reported lawmakers questioned the Iran war’s endgame; Trump was considering winding down operations, and Sen. Tillis called for authorization or a clear exit path.
terminal.description_medium: An Associated Press report published March 21, 2026, said lawmakers were questioning when, how and at what cost the Iran war would end. It reported that Trump was considering winding down military operations while outlining new goals. Sen. Thom Tillis said the administration needed to articulate a strategy and, around the 45-day mark, either authorization for continued military action or a clear exit path. The report does not establish that no exit plan existed.
terminal.description_long: An Associated Press report by Lisa Mascaro, published March 21, 2026, described lawmakers questioning when, how and at what cost the U.S. war with Iran would end. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told AP that the central question was what the campaign was meant to accomplish and called for a clearer articulation of its objectives. The report said President Donald Trump had said late Friday that he was considering “winding down” military operations while also outlining new objectives. It described congressional responses: Republicans had voted down several Democratic resolutions intended to halt the campaign, and lawmakers said the administration would need to present a more comprehensive strategy. Tillis said that near the 45-day mark the administration needed to articulate either authorization for the use of military force to sustain the campaign beyond that point or a clear path to exit. This supports describing congressional scrutiny of the war’s aims and endgame alongside Tillis’s stated expectation. It does not establish that no operational exit plan existed, that Congress formally demanded one, or that the campaign lacked all legal authorization. This proposal corrects the earlier wording that asserted Trump took the country to war “without one”: the report supports scrutiny and a request for clarity, not proof that no plan existed.

terminal.title: Trump Says U.S. Would Enter Iran to Excavate Uranium at Arizona Rally
terminal.description_short: At an Arizona rally, Trump said the U.S. would go into Iran to excavate uranium, according to AP’s video headline.
terminal.description_medium: At a Turning Point USA rally in Arizona, Trump spoke about the Iran war and said the United States would go into Iran to excavate uranium, according to AP’s video headline. AP’s description says he suggested Iran had agreed to hand over enriched uranium. NPR’s transcript reports cheers during his Iran remarks and attributes a record-low 39% approval rating to an average of polls.
terminal.description_long: President Donald Trump spoke at a Turning Point USA campaign-style rally in Arizona in April 2026, during a trip NPR described as an effort to build Republican support in battleground states before the midterm elections. NPR’s transcript places the appearance amid public opposition to the war in Iran and quotes Trump saying the United States had been defending Americans because Iran could not have a nuclear weapon; the report says the crowd cheered during that passage. The Associated Press video headline says Trump said the United States would go into Iran and excavate uranium, while the AP description says he suggested Iran had agreed to hand over enriched uranium. NPR also reports that an average of polls put Trump’s approval at 39%, described as a record low. The material supports an attributed account of these remarks and the event context. It does not establish that Iran agreed to transfer uranium, that the United States carried out an excavation or retrieval operation, or that the statement became policy.

supports: NPR published a recap dated April 18, 2026, describing Trump’s Arizona appearance at a campaign-style Turning Point USA event.
The report describes the crowd as friendly and says it cheered Trump’s remarks about the Iran war.
NPR reports an average of polls put Trump’s approval rating at a record-low 39%; it does not identify the component polls in the article.
limitations: The recap does not provide a complete transcript of Trump’s speech or identify the component polls.

supports: NPR’s transcript says Trump went to Arizona for a campaign-style rally with Turning Point USA.

NPR quotes Trump: ‘We are not ashamed of American might, and we do not hesitate to defend the American people, which is what we’ve been doing for the last two months because Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon.’
The transcript says the crowd cheered during that Iran passage.
NPR reports: ‘In an average of the polls, the president has hit a record low approval rating of 39%.’ It does not name the polls, survey dates, or question wording.
NPR describes Trump’s stated campaign purpose as seeking support in battleground states before the midterms.
limitations: This is an edited broadcast transcript excerpt, not a full transcript of the rally speech.

terminal.title: Project 2025 Medicaid Caps and Earlier Medicaid/SNAP Block-Grant Proposals
terminal.description_short: Project 2025 proposed Medicaid block grants or per-capita caps; a separate 2017 NWLC report discussed earlier proposals affecting Medicaid and SNAP.
terminal.description_medium: Georgetown’s Center for Children and Families reported that Project 2025 would cap federal Medicaid funding through block grants or per-capita limits. NWLC’s 2017 report discussed separate proposals to cap Medicaid and SNAP funding and projected possible effects. Neither supplied source documents a Trump administration conversion of both programs or realized effects.
terminal.description_long:
Georgetown’s Center for Children and Families described Project 2025 as a policy agenda for a potential second Trump administration and reported that it would convert federal Medicaid funding to block grants or per-capita caps. The article says the plan did not specify how the caps would initially be set or adjusted each year. It explains that fixed federal contributions would no longer track states’ actual costs and discusses risks if enrollment, health-care costs, or unexpected needs grew faster than capped funding. Those effects are projected risks, not reported outcomes.

The National Women’s Law Center’s 2017 report is separate and predates Project 2025. It discusses congressional proposals at that time to cap Medicaid and SNAP funding and analyzes possible effects on eligible people and state budgets. It does not establish that Project 2025 proposed converting SNAP. Neither supplied article documents a 2025 Trump administration conversion of Medicaid or SNAP, eliminated matching payments, required state service cuts, or realized harms.

supports: The article describes Project 2025 as an agenda for a potential second Trump administration.
It says the plan would convert federal Medicaid funding to block grants or per-capita caps.
It says the plan does not specify the caps’ initial amounts or annual adjustments and explains that caps would limit federal contributions regardless of states’ actual costs.
It presents effects from funding caps as projected risks, including failure to keep pace with enrollment, health-care costs, or unexpected needs.
limitations: The article does not document implementation by the Trump administration or realized effects.
It does not establish that Project 2025 proposed converting SNAP to a block grant.

supports: The May 22, 2017 report discusses then-current congressional proposals to cap Medicaid and SNAP funding through block grants and analyzes possible effects on eligible people, benefits, and state budgets.
The report describes possible effects as consequences of proposals, not observed outcomes of a 2025 administration action.
limitations: The report predates Project 2025 and cannot support attributing SNAP block-grant proposals to that blueprint.
It does not document implementation of the described proposals as a 2025 Trump administration action.

terminal.title: Trump Signs DHS Funding Bill Ending the Shutdown
terminal.description_short: Trump signed DHS funding legislation that ended the shutdown while excluding ICE and CBP Border Patrol from its appropriations.
terminal.description_medium: On April 30, 2026, Donald Trump signed a DHS funding measure that ended the shutdown. It funded most DHS agencies through fiscal year 2026, excluding ICE and CBP Border Patrol from its appropriations; employees of those agencies were then being paid under a prior reconciliation law. The bill provided $48 billion for covered agencies.
terminal.description_long:
On April 30, 2026, President Donald Trump signed a bill that funded most Department of Homeland Security operations and ended the agency’s shutdown. The measure provided Fiscal Year 2026 funding for covered DHS agencies, totaling $48 billion, while excluding Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection’s Border Patrol; employees of those agencies were being paid through the previous year’s reconciliation law. It identified funded components including the Federal Emergency Management Agency, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, Transportation Security Administration, Coast Guard, and Secret Service.

The measure also included oversight provisions addressing the administration’s immigration-related policies. It directed DHS to develop a uniform policy making federal law-enforcement personnel clearly identifiable, increased funding for DHS’s Office of Inspector General by $37 million, a 20 percent increase, and provided funding for the Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties and the Office of the Citizenship and Immigration Services Ombudsman. The congressional release said the action would restart federal employees’ paychecks and allow services, including FEMA disaster response and Coast Guard operations, to resume.

supports: The Trump File page says a 1996 Senate investigations committee recognized that the Semion Mogilevich Organization operated in the United States.

The page lists Robert Maxwell, Jacob Bogatin, David Bogatin, Mikhail Sheferovsky, Vyacheslav Ivankov, Vahtang Ubiriya, and Leib Yermolkin as Mogilevich associates, then asserts that at least two had ties to Donald Trump.
https://trumpfile.org/a-senate-hearing-c.limitations: This is the page’s own account. It does not identify which associates had Trump ties, describe those ties, or provide supporting evidence for that assertion in the entry.

supports: CNN published a May 16, 1996 report about Senate Governmental Affairs Committee testimony concerning Russian organized crime and alleged Russian-Italian Mafia cooperation.
CNN attributes the allegations to witnesses, including Michael Franzese, and reports officials’ testimony about criminal activity.
http://us.cnn.com/US/9605/16/russian.mob.limitations: CNN does not identify Semion Mogilevich or his organization, report a committee finding about that organization, or connect the hearing to Donald Trump. Its mention of hockey player Alexander Mogilny is not evidence about Semion Mogilevich.

supports: The official Senate hearing publication is titled “Russian Organized Crime in the United States” and records a hearing on May 15, 1996.
At printed page 86 (PDF page 92), the hearing publication lists “MOGILEViCH ORGANIZATION” and the name “Semion Mogielvich” (spelling as extracted from the PDF).
https://trumpfile.org/wp-content/uploads.limitations: The list establishes that the organization and name appear in the hearing publication; it does not by itself establish a formal committee finding or any connection to Donald Trump.

focused_rescue.method: Fetched the PDF linked from the supplied Trump File page and extracted its text; checked the title/date and the Mogilevich organization list at printed page 86 (PDF page 92).

blockers: Still missing: a reliable account identifying which Mogilevich associate or associates had a documented tie to Donald Trump, what that tie was, and evidence that connects this hearing to Trump. The Trump File page asserts that at least two associates had Trump ties but does not identify or substantiate them. The official hearing publication lists the Mogilevich Organization, but does not establish a formal Senate finding; any later use of this event should correct “Senate confirms” to wording that says the hearing publication lists the organization.
terminal.rationale: One focused source check resolved only the narrow question of whether the Senate hearing publication named the organization: its printed page 86 list does. CNN covers Russian organized crime testimony generally, while the Trump File page supplies an undocumented assertion about unnamed associates’ Trump ties. The evidence does not establish the Trump nexus required to complete this Trump-focused record, so the prior hold remains a hold and no reader-facing copy or impact score is proposed.

The page attributes to Litvinenko allegations about a plot against Boris Berezovsky and claims that Russian government and organized-crime roles were indistinguishable; these are claims reported by the page, not findings established by this source.
The page says Vladimir Putin did not attend and that Litvinenko was later arrested and fled Russia.
The page labels its broader collection as The Trump Timeline, but its account of this conference supplies no event-specific connection to Donald Trump.

supported_facts: The Trump File page is titled “Michael Caputo moves to Ukraine to aid Putin in political takeover” and dates the entry January 5, 2007.
Its caption states: “Michael Caputo leaves Miami Beach to move to Ukraine and help a politician’s campaign.”
limitations: This is the page making the Putin-directed-takeover claim; the supplied page text and caption do not independently substantiate Putin directing the work, a political takeover, or a Trump action.

supported_facts: Caputo testified: “in 2007, I lived briefly in Ukraine, in Kiev, and worked on a parliamentary election campaign for Bloc Lytvyn.”
He testified: “We ran against the President's party, managed by Paul Manafort. We won. Lytvyn was elected and later elected speaker of the Verkhovna.”
He separately testified: “I worked for the Trump campaign from late November 2015 to June 20, 2016.” This places his later Trump campaign work years after the Ukraine campaign.
limitations: The testimony supports the 2007 campaign work and later Trump campaign employment, but does not frame the 2007 work as a Trump action or establish that Putin directed it, that it produced a political takeover, or that it concerned media intimidation.

supported_facts: The House Intelligence Committee witness-transcripts index lists “Michael Caputo Testimony July 14, 2017” and links to the supplied testimony PDF.
limitations: The index identifies the transcript and its date; it does not add evidence connecting the 2007 campaign work to Trump, Putin, a takeover, or media intimidation.

terminal.title: Trump Orders Increased Transfers of Federal Assets to Local Police
terminal.description_short: Executive Order 14288 directs an increase in transfers of excess federal military and national-security assets to local law enforcement.
terminal.description_medium: On April 28, 2025, President Donald Trump issued Executive Order 14288. It directs the Attorney General and Defense Secretary to increase the provision of excess military and national-security assets to state and local law-enforcement agencies within 90 days. A cited opinion column relays the Legal Defense Fund’s concerns about aggressive policing and accountability. The order text alone does not show that transfers occurred or establish the column’s broader “police state” characterization.
terminal.description_long: On April 28, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14288, titled “Strengthening and Unleashing America’s Law Enforcement to Pursue Criminals and Protect Innocent Citizens.” Among several directives, the order tells the Attorney General and Secretary of Defense, in consultation with other agencies, to increase the provision of excess military and national-security assets to state and local law enforcement within 90 days. This is a direction to federal agencies; the order itself does not document how many assets were transferred, which departments received them, or how they were used. A July 2025 Times-Republican opinion column discussed the directive and relayed concerns from the Legal Defense Fund about possible aggressive policing and reduced accountability. Those concerns are attributed views about potential effects, not findings that misconduct occurred. The supplied sources do not show that the order reversed police consent decrees, violated constitutional rights, or implemented martial law. Such claims would require separate legal or implementation records. The supported account is therefore limited to the order’s asset-transfer directive and the debate the column reports.

supports: White House page identifies Executive Order 14288, dated April 28, 2025, and supplies the title retained in the long description.

Section 4(a): “Within 90 days of the date of this order, the Attorney General and the Secretary of Defense, in consultation with the Secretary of Homeland Security and the heads of agencies as appropriate, shall increase the provision of excess military and national security assets in local jurisdictions to assist State and local law enforcement.” Supports the described directive, responsible officials, affected agencies, assets, and timeframe.

Section 4(b) directs Defense, coordinating with the Attorney General, to determine how assets, training, non-lethal capabilities, and personnel could be used to prevent crime; it is a further direction, not evidence of completed transfers.

Section 3(b) directs the Attorney General to review covered consent decrees and related measures and modify, rescind, or seek to conclude those that unduly impede law-enforcement functions; it does not establish that any decree was actually reversed.
source_fact_map.limitations: The order establishes directives and deadlines; it does not identify completed transfers, recipients, quantities, uses, or effects, or find that constitutional rights were violated or martial law was implemented.

supports: The July 19, 2025 opinion column quotes the order’s excess-asset provision and says the Legal Defense Fund states the order directs federal resources to “promote aggressive policing tactics and further militarize local law enforcement agencies” and make accountability more difficult. This supports only the attribution that the column relays these concerns.
source_fact_map.limitations: Opinion commentary and attributed concerns; it does not document implementation, actual misconduct, legal findings, or the broader characterization as an established result.
The supplied URL redirected to the non-www host and returned HTTP 404 on October 4, 2026; it supports no factual claim.

terminal.title: TrumpFile Reports Two 2016 Airport Overlaps Between Trump Campaign and Rybolovlev Jets
terminal.description_short: TrumpFile reported two 2016 airport overlaps between a Trump campaign jet and Dmitry Rybolovlev’s aircraft; it says both men claimed they had never met.
terminal.description_medium: TrumpFile’s November 3, 2016 post said the Trump campaign’s jet and Dmitry Rybolovlev’s aircraft landed at the same airports in Las Vegas and Charlotte around the same time on October 30 and November 3. It said Trump was campaigning and that both men claimed they had never met. The account reports aircraft proximity, not a meeting or confirmed passenger overlap.
terminal.description_long: TrumpFile’s post, titled “Donald Trump and Dmitry Rybolovlev cross paths twice in a week,” reported two airport overlaps between the Trump campaign’s jet and an aircraft associated with Dmitry Rybolovlev. It said the planes landed at the same airports in Las Vegas and Charlotte, North Carolina, around the same time on October 30 and November 3, while Trump was campaigning. The post added that the aircraft shared the Charlotte tarmac for several hours before Trump left for a rally near Raleigh, and that a Rybolovlev spokesman declined to explain the Charlotte visit. It also said both men claimed they had never met and described whether the flights enabled contact as unresolved. This account supports a report of aircraft proximity on two occasions. It does not establish who was aboard, whether Trump and Rybolovlev were personally at either airport at the same time, whether they met or communicated, or whether the travel was coordinated.

terminal.title: Trump Addresses Dayton and El Paso Shootings in August 5 Remarks
terminal.description_short: On August 5, 2019, Trump addressed the Dayton and El Paso attacks, expressed sympathy for victims and survivors, and said he directed federal authorities to help.
terminal.description_medium: On August 5, 2019, President Donald Trump delivered White House remarks about the attacks in Dayton, Ohio, and El Paso, Texas. He said nine people were killed and 27 injured in Dayton, expressed sympathy for victims, families, and survivors, and said he had spoken with Ohio Governor Mike DeWine and Dayton Mayor Nan Whaley. Trump also said he directed federal authorities to provide any assistance required.
terminal.description_long: At 10:08 a.m. on August 5, 2019, President Donald Trump spoke in the White House Diplomatic Reception Room about the attacks in El Paso, Texas, and Dayton, Ohio. In describing Dayton, he said nine people had been killed, including the gunman’s sister, and 27 injured; these casualty figures are attributed to Trump’s remarks. He and the First Lady joined Americans in mourning victims, their families, and survivors. Trump said he had spoken with Ohio Governor Mike DeWine and Dayton Mayor Nan Whaley to express sadness and support. He also said he was in close contact with Attorney General William Barr and FBI Director Christopher Wray. Trump stated that he had directed federal authorities to provide any assistance required. The transcript documents his public response to the two attacks and the assistance directive he announced. This is the August 5 statement, distinct from the August 4 Dayton shooting itself. It does not assert that Trump caused the attack or that his response changed the investigation or the outcome.

Judge Beverly Martin dissented.","description_long":"On November 20, 2020, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit decided an appeal by licensed therapists Robert Otto and Julie Hamilton challenging ordinances adopted by the City of Boca Raton and Palm Beach County. The City’s ordinance exempted clergy and allowed supportive counseling for people undergoing gender transition. The majority held that the ordinances regulated speech based on its content and could not survive strict scrutiny under the First Amendment. It reversed the district court’s denial of a preliminary injunction and remanded for entry of an injunction consistent with the opinion. Judge Beverly Martin dissented, arguing that the ordinances regulated professional conduct. The ruling concerned those two local ordinances and the therapists’ preliminary-injunction appeal; it did not announce a nationwide policy. terminal.title: Eleventh Circuit Holds Boca Raton and Palm Beach County Conversion-Therapy Ordinances Violate the First Amendment
terminal.description_short: A divided Eleventh Circuit panel held that conversion-therapy ordinances in Boca Raton and Palm Beach County violated the First Amendment.
terminal.description_medium: On November 20, 2020, a divided Eleventh Circuit panel ruled in Otto v. City of Boca Raton that ordinances in Boca Raton and Palm Beach County restricting licensed therapists from providing sexual-orientation-change counseling to minors violated the First Amendment. The court treated the rules as content-based speech regulations that failed strict scrutiny. Judge Beverly Martin dissented.
terminal.description_long: On November 20, 2020, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit decided an appeal by licensed therapists Robert Otto and Julie Hamilton challenging ordinances adopted by the City of Boca Raton and Palm Beach County. The local rules restricted licensed therapists from providing sexual-orientation-change counseling to minors. The City’s ordinance exempted clergy and allowed supportive counseling for people undergoing gender transition. The majority held that the ordinances regulated speech based on its content and could not survive strict scrutiny under the First Amendment. It reversed the district court’s denial of a preliminary injunction and remanded for entry of an injunction consistent with the opinion. Judge Beverly Martin dissented, arguing that the ordinances regulated professional conduct. The ruling concerned those two local ordinances and the therapists’ preliminary-injunction appeal; it did not announce a nationwide policy. The official opinion identifies the panel as Martin, Britt Grant, and Barbara Lagoa.

supported_facts.quote: Boca Raton and Palm Beach County prohibit therapists from engaging in counseling or any therapy with a goal of changing a minor’s sexual orientation

supported_facts.fact: The majority held that the ordinances violated the First Amendment as content-based speech regulations that failed strict scrutiny.
supported_facts.quote: We hold that the challenged ordinances violate the First Amendment because they are content-based regulations of speech that cannot survive strict scrutiny.

supported_facts.fact: The court reversed the district court and remanded for entry of a preliminary injunction; Judge Martin dissented.
supported_facts.quote: We therefore REVERSE the district court’s order and REMAND for entry of a preliminary injunction consistent with this opinion. / MARTIN, Circuit Judge, dissenting:

supported_facts.fact: The City ordinance exempted clergy, and the ordinances permitted supportive counseling for people undergoing gender transition.
supported_facts.quote: The City’s ordinance applies to “any person who is licensed by the State of Florida to provide professional counseling,” except for clergy. / they expressly allow “counseling that provides support and assistance to a person undergoing gender transition.”

terminal.title: White House Spanish-Language Website and X Profile Taken Offline in 2025
terminal.description_short: White House Spanish-Language Website and X Profile Taken Offline in 2025
terminal.description_medium: Within hours of Donald Trump’s January 20, 2025 inauguration, the Spanish-language White House website was taken offline and showed a 404 error. An Associated Press report republished by PBS NewsHour also identified the White House’s Spanish-language X profile, @LaCasaBlanca, and a government reproductive-freedom page as disbanded. A White House spokesperson said the site was being edited and said the Spanish translation section would return; the report gave no restoration date.
terminal.description_long:
At about 4 p.m. Eastern on January 20, 2025, hours after Donald Trump’s inauguration, the Spanish versions of the White House website and social media accounts became unavailable, according to TrumpFile’s timeline. The Associated Press, in a report republished by PBS NewsHour, said the new administration took down the Spanish-language White House website; the site returned an “Error 404” message. The report named the White House’s Spanish-language X profile, @LaCasaBlanca, and the government page on reproductive freedom as also disbanded. It noted that Spanish pages for the Departments of Labor, Justice, and Agriculture remained available on Tuesday.

Asked about the change on the administration’s second day, principal deputy press secretary Harrison Fields said the White House was developing, editing, and tweaking its website, and that some archived content had gone dormant. He said the administration was committed to bringing the Spanish translation section back online and reloading dormant content “in a short timeline,” without specifying when. The contemporaneous reporting documents the initial outage and the administration’s stated plan; it does not establish a later restoration date or whether every affected page or account returned. The record therefore describes assets taken offline during the transition rather than a proven permanent shutdown.

supports: The timeline states that at approximately 4 p.m. Eastern, hours after Trump’s inauguration, Spanish versions of the White House website and social media accounts were removed from the internet.
The timeline says it would be updated if further context became available.
limitations: It does not explain the administration’s reason, identify the specific affected social accounts, or establish later restoration status.

supports: The indexed AP story excerpt reports the Spanish-language White House site was taken down within hours of the inauguration and displayed an Error 404 message.
The AP excerpt identifies @LaCasaBlanca and the reproductive-freedom government page as also disbanded; Spanish pages for Labor, Justice, and Agriculture remained available Tuesday.
The AP excerpt quotes Harrison Fields describing website development/editing, archived content going dormant, and a commitment to restore Spanish translation content.
limitations: A direct request returned HTTP 403; facts were checked against the accessible PBS republication below. The AP excerpt does not establish whether or when restoration later occurred.

supports: PBS NewsHour’s AP republication states: “Within hours of President Donald Trump’s inauguration, the new administration took down the Spanish-language version of the official White House website”; it says the site showed an “Error 404” message.

It states the Spanish White House X profile @LaCasaBlanca and the reproductive-freedom government page “also were disbanded,” while Spanish versions of the Labor, Justice, and Agriculture departments remained available Tuesday.

It quotes Harrison Fields: “We are in the process of developing, editing and tweaking the White House website”; archived content “went dormant”; and the administration was “committed to bringing back online the Spanish translation section of the website” and to reloading the content “in a short timeline.”
limitations: The contemporaneous report gives no specific restoration date and does not verify later restoration. It does not establish a quantified affected audience or downstream consequences.

The staged title and short description are adequate and preserved. The frozen wording “deletes Spanish website and social media accounts” is narrowed in the long copy to the specific assets reported, avoiding a claim that all Spanish-language government accounts were removed or that the shutdown was permanent. Later restoration status remains unknown in the sources, so the proposed copy states only the contemporaneous commitment and makes no claim that restoration occurred. terminal.title: Trump's 'Covfefe' Tweet Stayed Online for Nearly Six Hours
terminal.description_short: Trump tweeted “Despite the constant negative press covfefe” at 12:06 a.m. on May 31, 2017, deleted it before 6 a.m., then asked who could figure out “covfefe.”
terminal.description_medium: At 12:06 a.m. Eastern on May 31, 2017, Donald Trump tweeted, “Despite the constant negative press covfefe.” The Washington Post reported that he deleted the unfinished post at 5:48 a.m. and then asked, “Who can figure out the true meaning of ‘covfefe’ ??? Enjoy!” The word became a Twitter trend as users posted jokes and guesses.
terminal.description_long: At 12:06 a.m. Eastern on May 31, 2017, Donald Trump posted, “Despite the constant negative press covfefe.” The Washington Post described the message as a sentence fragment that ended abruptly. It remained on Twitter until 5:48 a.m., when Trump deleted it. While it was online, users guessed at the unfinished word and made jokes. The newspaper said “covfefe” became a trend, producing the “#covfefe” and “Rosebud” trending topics and a Twitter Moment. It also recounted users’ wordplay, including one person joking about ordering a grande “covfefe,” while some commenters defended the post as a possible human error. The article noted that Merriam-Webster’s site suggested words such as “coffee,” “coven,” and “cover” when searching for “covfefe.” After deleting the original, Trump posted: “Who can figure out the true meaning of ‘covfefe’ ??? Enjoy!” The follow-up invited speculation but did not explain the original wording. The reporting leaves Trump’s intended word or meaning unresolved.

supported_facts: The post appeared at 12:06 a.m. Eastern on May 31, 2017 and read “Despite the constant negative press covfefe.”
The article described the post as a sentence fragment that ended abruptly and reported its deletion at 5:48 a.m.
After deleting it, Trump posted “Who can figure out the true meaning of covfefe ??? Enjoy!”
Users made guesses and jokes; the article reported that covfefe and Rosebud were trending topics and that a Twitter Moment was created.
The article recounted that some users defended the post as a possible human error and reported Merriam-Webster suggestions including coffee, coven, and cover.
limitations: The article does not establish what Trump intended to write or the meaning of covfefe.
No policy or institutional consequence is established by this reporting.
The URL was attempted during this focused rescue but returned HTTP 402; no article text was available to verify its claims.
No public-copy claim relies on this source.

terminal.title: Trump Signs H-1B Proclamation Requiring $100,000 Payment for Certain New Petitions
terminal.description_short: Proclamation 10973 conditioned entry for certain H-1B workers on a $100,000 payment; the requirement began September 21, 2025, with exceptions.
terminal.description_medium: On September 19, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Proclamation 10973, restricting entry of certain H-1B workers unless a $100,000 payment accompanied the petition. It took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT on September 21. Employers had to obtain and retain proof of payment before filing petitions for workers outside the United States; the Homeland Security secretary could grant national-interest exceptions. White House guidance said it covered new petitions and did not change renewal fees.
terminal.description_long: On September 19, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Proclamation 10973, “Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers.” It restricted entry to the United States for certain H-1B specialty-occupation workers unless a $100,000 payment accompanied or supplemented the petition. The Homeland Security secretary could exempt an individual, a company’s workers, or an industry’s workers when hiring served the national interest and posed no threat to U.S. security or welfare. The proclamation took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT on September 21, 2025, and set an initial 12-month term absent extension. It directed employers to obtain and retain proof of payment before filing petitions for workers outside the United States, and assigned payment verification and implementation roles to the State and Homeland Security departments. The White House FAQ said the payment applied to new petitions submitted after the effective time, not previously issued visas or earlier petitions, and did not change renewal fees. The cited material documents the policy’s terms; it does not establish any later extension or its measured effects.

facts_supported: The supplied TrumpFile article is titled “Trump places $100K fee on H-1B visa applications” and is dated September 19, 2025.
It reports Trump’s statement and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s contemporaneous uncertainty about how the $100,000 amount would be charged.
source_fact_map.limitations: The article calls the instrument an executive order and describes the measure broadly as a fee on visa applications; the proclamation and White House FAQ below supply the more precise instrument and scope.

facts_supported: The document is Proclamation 10973, signed September 19, 2025, and titled “Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers.”
Section 1 establishes a $100,000 payment condition for covered H-1B workers’ entry, an effective time of 12:01 a.m. EDT on September 21, 2025, and a 12-month initial term absent extension.
Section 1(c) authorizes discretionary national-interest exceptions subject to the stated security and welfare condition.

Section 2 requires employers to obtain and retain payment documentation before filing covered petitions for workers outside the United States; it assigns verification and implementation roles to State and Homeland Security.
source_fact_map.limitations: The proclamation text does not establish whether it was later extended or the measured effects of the policy.

facts_supported: The White House FAQ dated September 21, 2025 says the payment applied to new H-1B petitions submitted after 12:01 a.m. EDT on September 21, 2025.
It says previously issued H-1B visas and earlier petitions were outside the measure, and that renewal fees were unchanged.
source_fact_map.limitations: The FAQ summarizes the rule and notes agency guidance; it does not itself provide detailed collection procedures beyond the proclamation.

terminal.rationale: The Federal Register proclamation and White House FAQ resolve the stated context gap: instrument, covered filing/entry scope, $100,000 payment, employer documentation, discretionary exception, effective time, and high-level agency responsibilities are supported. The copy corrects the original article’s “executive order” wording to Presidential Proclamation 10973 and narrows the broad “fee on applications” framing to covered new H-1B petitions and entry conditions. The prior short description was truncated, so this proposal supplies a complete short description and includes the official source URLs.

terminal.title: Trump Ends Canada Trade Talks and Announces a 10% Tariff Increase Over Ontario’s Reagan Ad
terminal.description_short: Trump said he was ending trade talks with Canada over Ontario’s Reagan ad and announced an additional 10% tariff, without specifying affected goods.
terminal.description_medium: On Oct. 23, 2025, Trump called Ontario’s Reagan ad “FAKE” and said he was ending trade negotiations with Canada. The next day, he suggested to reporters that the ad might have used AI, a claim not established by the sources. On Oct. 25, he announced an additional 10% tariff on Canada over the ad; Reuters reported that the affected goods were not specified.
terminal.description_long: Ontario’s provincial government aired a television advertisement using excerpts from former President Ronald Reagan’s 1987 radio address about tariffs. FactCheck.org found that the ad rearranged parts of the address and omitted context, but did not change Reagan’s broader anti-tariff message. On Oct. 23, 2025, Trump called the ad “FAKE,” said it was intended to interfere with pending Supreme Court tariff litigation, and announced that he was ending trade negotiations with Canada. The following day, he told reporters, “I guess it was AI or something”; this was an attributed suggestion, not evidence about how the advertisement was produced. On Oct. 25, Trump announced an additional 10% tariff on Canada, citing the ad. Reuters reported that he did not specify which goods the increase would cover and that most Canadian exports were exempt from tariffs under USMCA. Ontario Premier Doug Ford had said the province would pause the U.S. ad campaign on Monday after discussions with Prime Minister Mark Carney so trade talks could resume. This proposal records Trump’s announced actions and stated reasons; it does not say the tariff took effect or establish the later course of negotiations.

AP reported that Hegseth had fired more than a dozen top generals and admirals since taking office, and that more than a dozen other senior military leaders had either retired early or been removed from their posts.

The report named Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George, Army Gen. David Hodne, and Army Maj. Gen. William Green among leaders affected; it said Pentagon officials did not give reasons for George’s or Hodne’s and Green’s departures.
The report distinguishes firings from early retirements and other removals; it does not say all affected leaders were fired.

Since then, more than a dozen other top military generals and admirals have either retired early or been removed from their posts.
A reason for their departures also was not given.

terminal.title: NDSU Report Estimates $14.9 Billion China Tariff Shortfall
terminal.description_short: A May 2026 NDSU report estimates China’s 2025/26 retaliatory tariffs cut U.S. agricultural exports to China by $14.9 billion annualized.
terminal.description_medium: North Dakota State University researchers’ May 2026 report estimates that China’s 2025/26 retaliatory tariffs reduced U.S. agricultural exports to China by $14.9 billion on an annualized basis over March 2025–February 2026. The model assigns about $6.8 billion to soybeans. The estimate measures China-bound export shortfall, not net losses to U.S. farmers; the report says some shipments were redirected to other markets.
terminal.description_long: North Dakota State University’s May 2026 Agricultural Trade Monitor assesses China’s 2025/26 retaliatory tariffs on U.S. agricultural exports. Its structural-gravity analysis estimates an annualized $14.9 billion shortfall in U.S. shipments to China during March 2025–February 2026, relative to a 2024 export baseline. The report attributes the estimate to the combined Fentanyl and Reciprocal tariff layers imposed since March 2025 and assigns about $6.8 billion of the modeled shortfall to soybeans. It says the model controls for supply and demand shocks, seasonality, and global commodity trends. The $14.9 billion is a China-specific export shortfall, not lost exports overall or net harm to farmers; some shipments went to other markets. The report’s recommended citation dates it May 20, 2026, correcting the frozen March 4, 2025 record date. The prior “72% soybean collapse” wording is also corrected: NDSU lists soybean exports falling from $12.6 billion in 2024 to $3.1 billion in 2025; 72% is the combined share of five commodity categories in the modeled shortfall.

raw_line: {"record_id":"entry-4692","status":"hold","title":"Trump Pardons Binance Founder Changpeng Zhao Amid Reported Crypto-Ties Conflict Concerns","description_short":"Trump pardoned Binance founder Changpeng Zhao on October 21, 2025; reports raised conflict concerns over crypto-business ties.","description_medium":"The Justice Department records Donald Trump’s pardon of Binance founder Changpeng Zhao as dated October 21, 2025. Zhao pleaded guilty in November 2023 to failing to monitor money laundering at Binance and served a four-month sentence. Al Jazeera reported close dealings between Binance and the Trump family’s World Liberty Financial and said some viewed the pardon as a conflict of interest. Those reported ties raise concerns but do not establish that executives bought clemency.","description_long":"The Justice Department’s clemency register lists President Donald Trump’s pardon of Binance founder Changpeng Zhao under October 21, 2025, and identifies the offense as failure to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program. The register lists a four-month prison sentence and a $50 million fine. Al Jazeera reported that Zhao pleaded guilty in November 2023 to one count of not monitoring money laundering at Binance and served a four-month sentence. The report also describes business ties between Binance and World Liberty Financial, the crypto company Trump and members of his family own: World Liberty launched its USD1 stablecoin on Binance’s blockchain in March 2025, and Binance promoted the coin. terminal.title: Trump Pardons Binance Founder Changpeng Zhao Amid Reported Crypto-Ties Conflict Concerns
terminal.description_short: Trump pardoned Binance founder Changpeng Zhao on October 21, 2025; reports raised conflict concerns over crypto-business ties.
terminal.description_medium: The Justice Department records Donald Trump’s pardon of Binance founder Changpeng Zhao as dated October 21, 2025. Zhao pleaded guilty in November 2023 to failing to monitor money laundering at Binance and served a four-month sentence. Al Jazeera reported close dealings between Binance and the Trump family’s World Liberty Financial and said some viewed the pardon as a conflict of interest. Those reported ties raise concerns but do not establish that executives bought clemency.
terminal.description_long: The Justice Department’s clemency register lists President Donald Trump’s pardon of Binance founder Changpeng Zhao under October 21, 2025, and identifies the offense as failure to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program. The register lists a four-month prison sentence and a $50 million fine. Al Jazeera reported that Zhao pleaded guilty in November 2023 to one count of not monitoring money laundering at Binance and served a four-month sentence. The report also describes business ties between Binance and World Liberty Financial, the crypto company Trump and members of his family own: World Liberty launched its USD1 stablecoin on Binance’s blockchain in March 2025, and Binance promoted the coin. Al Jazeera says some viewed the pardon as a conflict of interest. The available records confirm the pardon and describe those business ties, but do not establish that the ties caused the clemency decision or that Zhao or executives bought it. The entry therefore records the pardon and reported conflict concern without presenting a quid pro quo as fact.

terminal.description_long: In January 2016, Donald Trump held a televised Iowa fundraiser for veterans instead of attending a Republican debate. The event raised about $5.6 million. A contemporaneous account said about $2.8 million went to the Trump Foundation, while private donors gave the remainder directly to veterans’ charities. The New York attorney general later said Trump and the Foundation admitted that the event was a campaign event and that the Foundation gave the campaign control over the timing, amounts, and recipients of the $2.8 million raised through it. NPR reported that court documents said the Foundation’s $2.82 million from the fundraiser was used for Trump’s campaign and disbursed by campaign staff, rather than by the Foundation; it also reported that the money eventually reached charities supporting veterans. The 2019 damages order was the later resolution of the Foundation case, not an event that took place on the fundraiser date.

It reported that internal communications identified the proposal as an immediate priority. The story also explained that the Act authorizes a president to deploy the military for domestic law enforcement.\n\nThe account describes conditional planning, not an adopted campaign policy or an order. terminal.title: Washington Post Reports Trump Allies Drafted Conditional Day-One Insurrection Act Plans
terminal.description_short: The Washington Post reported in November 2023 that Trump allies were drafting conditional day-one plans to invoke the Insurrection Act against civil demonstrations.
terminal.description_medium: On Nov. 6, 2023, The Washington Post reported that Trump associates were drafting plans to potentially invoke the Insurrection Act on the first day of a possible second term, allowing military deployment against civil demonstrations. The report attributes planning to his associates and Project 2025; it does not establish a public promise by Trump, an adopted policy, or Pentagon preparations.
terminal.description_long:
On Nov. 6, 2023, The Washington Post reported that Donald Trump’s associates were drafting plans to potentially invoke the Insurrection Act on the first day of a possible second term, allowing military deployment against civil demonstrations. The article attributed the plans to Trump allies and described Project 2025 as developing a plan, including draft executive orders, for domestic military deployment under the Act. It reported that internal communications identified the proposal as an immediate priority. The story also explained that the Act authorizes a president to deploy the military for domestic law enforcement.

The account describes conditional planning, not an adopted campaign policy or an order. It does not establish that Trump publicly promised to invoke the Act, that the Act was invoked, or that troops were deployed. The supplied record’s additional claims about mass deportation, protest suppression as a purpose, and Pentagon officials or military lawyers preparing for possible unlawful orders are not established by this report and are omitted.

quotes: Donald Trump and his allies have begun mapping out specific plans for using the federal government to punish critics and opponents should he win a second term, with the former president naming individuals he wants to investigate or prosecute and his associates drafting plans to potentially invoke the Insurrection Act on his first day in office to allow him to deploy the military against civil demonstrations.

Dubbed “Project 2025,” the group is developing a plan, to include draft executive orders, that would deploy the military domestically under the Insurrection Act, according to a person involved in those conversations and internal communications reviewed by The Washington Post. The law, last updated in 1871, authorizes the president to deploy the military for domestic law enforcement.
The proposal was identified in internal discussions as an immediate priority, the communications showed.
supports: The Nov. 6, 2023 report attributes conditional first-day Insurrection Act planning to Trump’s associates if he won a second term.
The report says the contemplated deployment was against civil demonstrations.
The report describes Project 2025 developing draft executive orders for domestic military deployment and says internal communications called the proposal an immediate priority.
limitations: The report does not establish that Trump himself publicly promised to invoke the Act, that the plan became adopted campaign policy, or that an order, invocation, or deployment occurred.
The report does not support the staged claims that the purpose was mass deportation or protest suppression, or that Pentagon officials or military lawyers prepared for possible unlawful orders.

The filing cited Trump’s history of social media posts about judges, lawyers and witnesses in his cases, including a Truth Social message stating, “If you go after me, I’m coming after you.” Trump’s defense described the post as political speech and contested the request. This procedural request concerned access to evidence exchanged in discovery; it was not itself a gag order covering all public statements and did not establish that the posts were criminal conduct. Other reporting in September 2023 described a separate request to restrict statements about participants in the election case. The supplied Washington Post link is an October 2023 catalogue, but its article body was not readable in the focused review. terminal.description_short: Trump granted Drew “Bo” Brownstein a full pardon in January 2021 after his securities-fraud conviction.
terminal.description_medium: On January 20, 2021, the White House announced that President Donald Trump had granted Drew “Bo” Brownstein a full pardon. DOJ’s index lists his securities-fraud conviction and a sentence of one year and one day in prison, three years of supervised release, and a $7,500 fine. The Colorado Sun reported that Brownstein ran a Denver hedge fund and pleaded guilty to illegal stock trading. The sources do not establish that donations influenced the pardon.
terminal.description_long: On January 20, 2021, the archived White House press secretary’s statement announced a full pardon for Drew Brownstein and said he had been convicted of insider trading and had paid his fines and forfeitures. The Justice Department’s pardon index lists Drew Kallman Brownstein under its January 19, 2021 grants. It identifies the Southern District of New York case as securities fraud and records a sentence of one year and one day in prison, three years of supervised release, and a $7,500 fine. The Colorado Sun reported that Brownstein ran a Denver hedge fund, pleaded guilty in 2011 to illegal stock trading, and was pardoned as Trump prepared to leave office. These sources establish the clemency event and Brownstein’s conviction. They do not establish the frozen description’s claim that associates donated to Trump-affiliated PACs, that contributions affected the decision, or that clemency was exchanged for donations. Those claims and the Government Corruption framing are removed from this narrowed proposal; no causal or donor relationship is asserted.

raw_line: {"record_id":"entry-5698","status":"pass","title":"NARA Worked With Trump Representatives to Locate Records and Transfer 15 Boxes","description_short":"NARA said it worked with Trump representatives in 2021 to locate untransferred presidential records; in January 2022 it arranged transport of 15 boxes from Mar-a-Lago.","description_medium":"NARA said it worked during 2021 with Trump representatives to locate presidential records not transferred at the end of his administration. A representative told the agency in December 2021 that some records had been located, after which NARA arranged secure transport to Washington. Separately, NARA said it arranged transport of 15 boxes of presidential records from Mar-a-Lago in mid-January 2022; representatives said they were continuing to search for additional records.","description_long":"The National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) described its work with representatives of former President Donald Trump to locate presidential records that had not been transferred at the end of his administration. NARA said it obtained their cooperation during 2021. The agency reported that in December 2021, a representative told it that some records had been located; NARA then arranged secure transport of those records to Washington. NARA also said that in mid-January 2022 it arranged transport from Mar-a-Lago to the Archives of 15 boxes containing presidential records, following discussions with Trump’s representatives during 2021. The agency said the representatives were continuing to search for additional presidential records belonging to the National Archives. terminal.title: NARA Worked With Trump Representatives to Locate Records and Transfer 15 Boxes
terminal.description_short: NARA said it worked with Trump representatives in 2021 to locate untransferred presidential records; in January 2022 it arranged transport of 15 boxes from Mar-a-Lago.
terminal.description_medium: NARA said it worked during 2021 with Trump representatives to locate presidential records not transferred at the end of his administration. A representative told the agency in December 2021 that some records had been located, after which NARA arranged secure transport to Washington. Separately, NARA said it arranged transport of 15 boxes of presidential records from Mar-a-Lago in mid-January 2022; representatives said they were continuing to search for additional records.
terminal.description_long: The National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) described its work with representatives of former President Donald Trump to locate presidential records that had not been transferred at the end of his administration. NARA said it obtained their cooperation during 2021. The agency reported that in December 2021, a representative told it that some records had been located; NARA then arranged secure transport of those records to Washington. NARA also said that in mid-January 2022 it arranged transport from Mar-a-Lago to the Archives of 15 boxes containing presidential records, following discussions with Trump’s representatives during 2021. The agency said the representatives were continuing to search for additional presidential records belonging to the National Archives. NARA stated that, under the Presidential Records Act, these records should have been transferred from the White House at the end of the administration in January 2021. It also said NARA officials did not visit or ‘raid’ the Mar-a-Lago property. This account documents the agency’s reported search and transfer timeline; it does not identify individual records beyond the 15 boxes or provide dates for each communication with Trump’s representatives.

terminal.title: Trump Announces 2024 Campaign
terminal.description_short: Donald Trump announced a 2024 presidential campaign at Mar-a-Lago on November 15, 2022.
terminal.description_medium: Donald Trump announced his 2024 presidential candidacy at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, on November 15, 2022, one week after the midterm elections. Reuters described the launch as a bid to regain the presidency and get ahead of potential Republican rivals. Trump spoke for a little more than an hour to hundreds of supporters and critiqued President Joe Biden’s record.
terminal.description_long: On November 15, 2022, Donald Trump announced his candidacy for president in 2024 at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida. Reuters reported that he made the announcement one week after the midterm elections, when Republicans had failed to win as many seats in Congress as they had hoped. The report characterized the launch as a bid to regain the presidency and get ahead of potential Republican rivals, with a possible rematch against President Joe Biden. Trump spoke for a little more than an hour to hundreds of supporters in a ballroom decorated with chandeliers and American flags. He told the phone-waving crowd, which included family members, donors and former staffers, that he was announcing his candidacy. Reuters reported that he critiqued Biden’s presidency and reviewed his own policy achievements. The report also describes proposals from the speech, including the death penalty for drug dealers and rehiring military members dismissed for refusing COVID-19 vaccinations.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: PALM BEACH, Fla., Nov 15 (Reuters) - Donald Trump, who has mounted relentless attacks on the integrity of U.S. voting since his 2020 election defeat, on Tuesday launched a bid to regain the presidency in 2024, aiming to pre-empt potential Republican rivals.
supports: The campaign launch and Reuters's description of its political aim: regaining the presidency and pre-empting potential Republican rivals.

terminal.title: Trump’s Hurricane Maria visit to Puerto Rico included paper-towel distribution
terminal.description_short: During Trump’s October 2017 Puerto Rico visit after Hurricane Maria, he handed out flashlights and tossed paper-towel rolls to a crowd at a church distributing relief supplies.
terminal.description_medium: On October 3, 2017, Trump visited Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria. At a Guaynabo church distributing relief supplies, he handed out flashlights and tossed rolls of paper towels into a crowd, the Associated Press reported. Around 200 people cheered there, and Trump called them “Great people.”
terminal.description_long: President Donald Trump visited Puerto Rico on October 3, 2017, after Hurricane Maria struck the island on September 20. The Associated Press reported that Trump toured part of the damage before stopping at a church in Guaynabo being used to distribute relief supplies. The church was in an upscale neighborhood described as among the fastest to recover; around 200 people cheered, and many crowded around him for cellphone photos. Trump handed out flashlights and tossed rolls of paper towels into the crowd. He told those present, “There’s a lot of love in this room, a lot of love,” and called them “Great people.” Earlier in the visit, he praised the federal relief effort and said the job done there was “really nothing short of a miracle.” The AP account described people outside San Juan still struggling to find water and food; it also reported that Puerto Rico’s governor said the official death toll rose from 16 to 34 late that Tuesday. Trump’s itinerary included stops with local residents and service members aboard the USS Kearsarge.

supported_facts: The AP account, published on October 3, 2017, reports Trump’s Puerto Rico visit that Tuesday, after Maria hit the island on September 20.

It reports that Trump toured damage, stopped at a Guaynabo church distributing supplies in a neighborhood described as recovering quickly, and handed out flashlights and tossed paper towels as around 200 people cheered.
It quotes Trump praising the gathering and calling the recovery a miracle; it also describes people still seeking food and water and reports the governor’s then-current death count of 34, up from 16.
It says Trump also visited local residents and service members aboard USS Kearsarge.

terminal.title: Trump Signed Executive Order 13780, Revising Travel and Refugee Restrictions
terminal.description_short: Trump signed Executive Order 13780 on March 6, 2017; it temporarily restricted entry for nationals of six countries and paused refugee admissions.
terminal.description_medium: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780 on March 6, 2017; it took effect March 16. The order suspended entry for 90 days for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to stated limits, exceptions and waivers. It separately suspended refugee travel and decisions on refugee-status applications for 120 days and set a 50,000-person ceiling for fiscal-year 2017 admissions. In the Hawaii case, the Ninth Circuit affirmed some injunction provisions and vacated others.
terminal.description_long:
President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780, “Protecting the Nation From Foreign Terrorist Entry Into the United States,” on March 6, 2017. It revoked Executive Order 13769 when it took effect at 12:01 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time on March 16. Section 2 suspended entry for 90 days for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen. Section 3 limited that restriction to people outside the United States who lacked a valid visa at 5 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on January 27 and still lacked one on the order’s effective date. The order listed exceptions, including lawful permanent residents, certain dual nationals, people granted asylum and refugees already admitted, and allowed case-by-case waivers.

Section 6 separately suspended refugee travel and decisions on refugee-status applications under the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program for 120 days, subject to exceptions and waivers, and limited fiscal-year 2017 admissions to 50,000. In the Hawaii case, the Ninth Circuit affirmed parts of a preliminary injunction blocking the entry suspension, refugee-program pause and admissions cap, vacated other parts concerning internal reviews and the President, and remanded. This appellate disposition describes the Hawaii case; it does not combine that case with the separate Maryland litigation.

supported_facts.supports: The order is a Presidential Document by the Executive Office of the President.

supported_facts.quote:
THE WHITE HOUSE,

March 6, 2017.
supported_facts.supports: The order is dated March 6, 2017.

supported_facts.quote: This order is effective at 12:01 a.m., eastern daylight time on March 16, 2017.
supported_facts.supports: The order took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT on March 16, 2017.

supported_facts.quote: Executive Order 13769 of January 27, 2017, is revoked as of the effective date of this order.
supported_facts.supports: EO 13780 revoked EO 13769 on its effective date.

supported_facts.quote: The unrestricted entry into the United States of nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen would be detrimental to the interests of the United States. I therefore direct that the entry into the United States of nationals of those six countries be suspended for 90 days from the effective date of this order, subject to the limitations, waivers, and exceptions set forth in sections 3 and 12 of this order.
supported_facts.supports: Section 2 suspended entry for 90 days for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to limitations, waivers and exceptions.

supported_facts.quote: The suspension of entry pursuant to section 2 of this order shall apply only to foreign nationals of the designated countries who:
supported_facts.supports: Section 3 limited the entry suspension to a defined class.

supported_facts.quote: did not have a valid visa at 5:00 p.m., eastern standard time on January 27, 2017
supported_facts.supports: The order included the January 27 visa-status cutoff.

supported_facts.quote: any lawful permanent resident of the United States
supported_facts.supports: Lawful permanent residents were exempt.

supported_facts.quote: any dual national of a country designated under section 2 of this order when the individual is traveling on a passport issued by a non-designated country
supported_facts.supports: A listed exception covered certain dual nationals.

supported_facts.quote: any foreign national who has been granted asylum
supported_facts.supports: People granted asylum were exempt.

supported_facts.quote: any refugee who has already been admitted to the United States
supported_facts.supports: Refugees already admitted were exempt.

supported_facts.quote: The Secretary of State shall suspend travel of refugees into the United States under the USRAP, and the Secretary of Homeland Security shall suspend decisions on applications for refugee status, for 120 days after the effective date of this order, subject to waivers pursuant to subsection (c) of this section.
supported_facts.supports: Section 6 suspended refugee travel and refugee-status application decisions for 120 days, subject to waivers.

supported_facts.quote: I hereby proclaim that the entry of more than 50,000 refugees in fiscal year 2017 would be detrimental to the interests of the United States, and thus suspend any entries in excess of that number until such time as I determine that additional entries would be in the national interest.
supported_facts.supports: Section 6 suspended refugee admissions above 50,000 for fiscal year 2017.
The Federal Register identifies the instrument as Executive Order 13780, supporting the policy-stage classification.

supported_facts.quote: We affirm in part and vacate in part the district court’s preliminary injunction order. As to the remaining Defendants, we affirm the injunction as to Section 2(c), suspending entry of nationals from the six designated countries for 90 days; Section 6(a), suspending USRAP for 120 days; and Section 6(b), capping the entry of refugees to 50,000 in the fiscal year 2017.
supported_facts.supports: In the Hawaii appeal, the Ninth Circuit affirmed the injunction as to the entry suspension, refugee-program suspension and fiscal-year 2017 cap.

supported_facts.quote: We vacate the portions of the injunction that prevent the Government from conducting internal reviews, as otherwise directed in Sections 2 and 6, and the injunction to the extent that it runs against the President. We remand the case to the district court with instructions to re-issue a preliminary injunction consistent with this opinion.
supported_facts.supports: The Ninth Circuit vacated parts concerning internal reviews and the President, then remanded for a revised injunction.

supported_facts.quote: need not consider the constitutional claims here.
supported_facts.supports: The Ninth Circuit opinion did not decide constitutional claims and does not support saying it held EO 13780 likely violated the Establishment Clause.

limitations: This is the Ninth Circuit opinion in the Hawaii case; it does not establish the disposition of separate Maryland litigation.

frozen_original.synopsis: After federal courts blocked the original Muslim ban, Trump signed a revised version on March 6, 2017, Executive Order 13780, which removed Iraq from the list and added exemptions for green card holders and existing visa holders. Courts again blocked the order, with federal judges in Hawaii and Maryland issuing nationwide injunctions before it could take effect. The Fourth and Ninth Circuit Courts of Appeals upheld the injunctions, ruling the order likely violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. The administration framed the continued legal battles as judicial overreach. Critics saw the second version as merely cosmetic changes to an unconstitutional religious targeting policy.

proposal.description_long: On March 6, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780, “Protecting the Nation from Foreign Terrorist Entry into the United States,” replacing his January order. The revised order suspended entry for 90 days by nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to stated exceptions, and set a separate 120-day pause on refugee admissions. Iraq was no longer among the six countries. The order stated an effective time of March 16, 2017. Before that date, a federal district court in Hawaii temporarily blocked key provisions; a Maryland district court also enjoined parts of the order, and the government appealed. The Ninth Circuit’s opinion concerns the scope of the Hawaii injunction and should not be collapsed into the separate Maryland case. The order text and opinions are the relevant evidence for its provisions and litigation chronology. The AP URL attached to the original entry is a fact-check about Trump’s tweets and votes, not this order, so it cannot substantiate the existing description. This account describes the order and court challenges without treating the different injunctions as one ruling or suggesting the entire order was permanently invalidated at that stage.

terminal.description_long: On June 20, 2025, the Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division announced a nationwide suspension of enforcement for all provisions introduced in the 2024 H-2A Farmworker Protection Rule. Field Assistance Bulletin 2025-2 directed staff to stop enforcing that rule and to assess employer compliance under the regulations in effect on June 27, 2024; the bulletin made the suspension effective immediately. The Department said court injunctions had already interrupted implementation and created legal uncertainty and operational challenges for farmers using the H-2A program. It said litigation continued while it considered further regulatory action. The 2024 rule covered the H-2A temporary agricultural labor certification program and included protections for foreign farmworkers, including workplace-organizing protections. The estimate concerns fees accumulated by entities behind the coin, not a documented $100 million payment by foreign buyers.
terminal.description_long: Donald Trump launched the $TRUMP memecoin on Jan. 17, 2025, three days before his inauguration. Reuters reported that the token quickly surged, reaching a market capitalization above $14.5 billion on Jan. 19. In a Feb. 3 report, Reuters cited estimates from three blockchain analysis firms that the token generated between $86 million and $100 million in trading fees by Jan. 30, less than two weeks after launch. Reuters described those fees as accumulated by entities behind the coin. This reported fee total is distinct from the frozen description’s claim that the initial trading surge “raised over $100 million”: the source estimates trading fees over the following period, not a $100 million launch-day raise. It also does not establish that anonymous wallet owners were foreign, document a hidden payment channel, or report that the SEC declined to investigate. The revised entry therefore retains the launch and fee story while removing unsupported claims about buyer nationality, foreign payments, and an SEC decision.
