terminal.description_long: During 2021, the National Archives and Records Administration worked with Donald Trump’s representatives to locate presidential records that had not been transferred when his administration ended. In statements issued on February 7 and 8, 2022, NARA explained the sequence leading to the return of 15 boxes from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property in Florida. A representative informed the agency in December 2021 that some records had been located. NARA then arranged secure transport to Washington, receiving the boxes in mid-January 2022. Trump’s representatives also told NARA that they were continuing to search for additional presidential records belonging to the Archives. The agency said these records should have been transferred from the White House at the end of Trump’s administration in January 2021 under the Presidential Records Act. Archivist David Ferriero emphasized that complete presidential records enable public accountability and that NARA pursues records improperly removed or not appropriately transferred. NARA said its officials had not visited or raided Mar-a-Lago to collect these boxes.

terminal.title: Trump Announces 2024 Campaign
terminal.description_short: Donald Trump announced a 2024 presidential campaign at Mar-a-Lago on November 15, 2022.
terminal.description_medium: Donald Trump announced his 2024 presidential campaign at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, on November 15, 2022. The launch came one week after the midterm elections and marked his third White House bid. He criticized President Biden and promoted his own administration’s record. ABC News reported that some aides suggested he believed candidacy would shield him from investigations; legal experts disputed that premise.
terminal.description_long: Donald Trump announced his third presidential campaign at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, on November 15, 2022. He presented another run for the White House as a national comeback and criticized President Joe Biden while promoting his own administration’s record. The launch came a week after Republicans performed worse than expected in the midterm elections. ABC News described an hour-long address in which Trump portrayed his presidency as a period of success and Biden’s tenure as a time of hardship. He also told supporters that his campaign would face attacks and persecution but would persevere. The announcement occurred while Trump faced multiple criminal and civil investigations, including federal inquiries concerning January 6 and documents recovered at Mar-a-Lago. ABC News reported that some aides suggested Trump believed declaring his candidacy would shield him from investigations. The report also said many legal experts rejected the idea that running would provide special protection. That attributed account establishes discussion of a possible legal strategy without proving Trump’s motive or an actual legal shield.

terminal.title: Trump’s Hurricane Maria Response in Puerto Rico: Visit, Relief Challenges and Later Mortality Estimate
terminal.description_short: Trump’s October 2017 Puerto Rico visit after Hurricane Maria included a paper-towel distribution at a relief center.
terminal.description_medium: After Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017, Trump visited on October 3 and tossed paper towels to residents. He had authorized a Jones Act shipping waiver on September 28. GAO later found staffing, logistics and infrastructure failures slowed FEMA’s response. An August 2018 George Washington University report estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 through February 2018.
terminal.description_long: Donald Trump visited Puerto Rico on October 3, 2017, after Hurricane Maria devastated the island in September. Reuters photographed him tossing rolls of paper towels into a crowd of residents affected by the storm at a chapel in San Juan. The visit followed his September 28 authorization of a Jones Act waiver intended to expedite relief supplies. ABC News reported criticism of the pace of aid and of the administration’s earlier failure to waive the shipping restrictions. A September 2018 Government Accountability Office report documented challenges that slowed and complicated FEMA’s response. Successive hurricanes created staffing shortages; the territories’ distance from the mainland complicated deployment of personnel and supplies; and damaged power, communications and local response systems required FEMA to assume duties ordinarily performed by territorial authorities. Separately, George Washington University researchers published a report in August 2018 estimating 2,975 excess deaths associated with Maria between September 2017 and February 2018. Their statistical analysis compared observed mortality with an expected baseline, adjusting for age, sex and migration. The estimate describes deaths associated with the hurricane and its aftermath; it does not assign those deaths to Trump’s visit or quantify the contribution of particular federal decisions.

proposal.description_long: Hurricane Maria made landfall in Puerto Rico in September 2017 and caused widespread damage to infrastructure, housing and communications. President Donald Trump visited the island on October 3. During a stop at a relief center, he tossed rolls of paper towels to people gathered there, an action that attracted criticism and became a prominent image of the visit. The federal response faced documented operational problems. The Government Accountability Office later reported that sequential disasters created staffing shortages, logistical challenges impeded the rapid deployment of personnel and supplies, and damage to local systems required FEMA to assume functions normally handled by territorial authorities. Separately, a George Washington University study estimated 2,975 excess deaths associated with Hurricane Maria through August 2018; GAO described that figure as Puerto Rico’s then-current official count. “Excess deaths” compares observed deaths with an expected baseline and should not be conflated with a count of deaths individually certified as directly caused by the storm. These sources support the visit, the distribution scene, response challenges and the later mortality estimate. They do not establish that the paper-towel event caused FEMA delays, nor do they provide support for every claim about the Jones Act or funding transfers in the original description. The title is narrowed to the documented visit; the response and mortality context is stated with attribution.
proposal.description_medium: Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017. Trump visited on October 3 and tossed paper towels to people at a relief center. GAO later found that staffing, logistics and infrastructure problems complicated FEMA’s response. A George Washington University study estimated 2,975 excess deaths through August 2018; this is an excess-mortality estimate, not a count of deaths individually attributed to the storm. The evidence does not connect the paper-towel scene to response delays.

frozen_original.synopsis: Trump's administration response to Hurricane Maria, which devastated Puerto Rico in September 2017, was widely condemned as catastrophically inadequate. Trump visited the island and infamously threw paper towels into a crowd of disaster survivors at a distribution center, treating a deadly emergency as a photo opportunity. The death toll from the hurricane eventually reached nearly 3,000, but Trump repeatedly dismissed estimates above single digits as a Democratic conspiracy. The administration was slow to waive the Jones Act to allow foreign ships to bring supplies, delayed FEMA deployment, and diverted funds from FEMA to immigration enforcement. An independent study by George Washington University confirmed the nearly 3,000 death estimate, which Trump publicly attacked.

proposal.description_long: On September 6, 2023, former President Donald Trump answered radio host Hugh Hewitt’s question about why he had not fired Anthony Fauci, whom Hewitt described as a major criticism of Trump’s pandemic response. Trump said Fauci was a civil servant and that he was “not allowed” to fire him. He also said Fauci would tell him things that he often did not follow, called Fauci “not a big player in my administration,” and said Fauci became a big player under President Biden. In the same interview, Trump criticized Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis over pandemic restrictions, saying DeSantis had closed Florida’s beaches and the state. Fox News reported that the exchange occurred during the 2024 Republican primary contest, when DeSantis was Trump’s closest opponent. This account records the statements and their interview context; it does not endorse Trump’s explanation of employment rules or his assessment of Fauci’s influence.
proposal.description_medium: In a September 2023 interview with Hugh Hewitt, Donald Trump said he was not allowed to fire Anthony Fauci, called him a civil servant, and said Fauci was not a “big player” in his administration. Trump added that Fauci became more influential under President Biden. The account reports Trump’s remarks without endorsing his explanation of federal employment rules.

Trump called for Fauci to be prosecuted and jailed. Congress investigated the NIH grants and found no evidence of deliberate pathogen creation. Trump's attacks on Fauci generated death threats against the scientist and his family, requiring permanent security protection.

terminal.description_short: Executive Order 13780 imposed temporary entry restrictions on nationals of six countries and paused refugee admissions in 2017.
terminal.description_medium: On March 6, 2017, Trump signed Executive Order 13780, replacing his first travel order. It directed a 90-day entry suspension for nationals of six countries, with exceptions, and a 120-day refugee pause. Iraq was removed from the covered list. Hawaii and Maryland courts blocked key provisions in separate cases. The Fourth Circuit upheld restrictions on enforcement on constitutional grounds; the Ninth Circuit relied on immigration statutes.
terminal.description_long:
On March 6, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780, replacing his January travel order. It directed a 90-day entry suspension for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to exceptions and discretionary waivers. Iraq was removed from the covered-country list. The restriction applied to specified people outside the United States who lacked valid visas at the dates set out in the order. Lawful permanent residents and dual nationals traveling on passports from non-designated countries were among those exempted. A separate provision directed a 120-day suspension of refugee travel and refugee-status decisions, subject to waivers. The scheduled effective date was March 16.

The litigation proceeded through separate cases. Hawaii issued a temporary restraining order against Sections 2 and 6 on March 15, followed by a preliminary injunction on March 29. Maryland enjoined Section 2(c) on March 16. On May 25, the Fourth Circuit substantially upheld the Maryland injunction based on the plaintiffs’ likely success under the Establishment Clause. On June 12, the Ninth Circuit largely upheld the Hawaii injunction on statutory grounds, while narrowing its scope. On June 26, the Supreme Court partly stayed the injunctions, permitting enforcement against people without a credible claim of a bona fide relationship with a person or entity in the United States.

terminal.title: Court Orders Trump to Pay $2 Million for Trump Foundation Misuse
terminal.description_short: A November 2019 court order required Trump to pay $2 million after misuse of Trump Foundation funds for his political interests.
terminal.description_medium: On November 7, 2019, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced a court order requiring Donald Trump to pay $2 million in damages for misuse of Trump Foundation assets during the 2016 campaign. Trump admitted misusing charitable funds. Settlements also imposed restrictions on future charitable service and directed the dissolved Foundation’s remaining assets to independent charities.
terminal.description_long:
On November 7, 2019, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced that the New York Supreme Court had ordered Donald Trump to pay $2 million in damages for improperly using charitable assets to advance his political interests during the 2016 presidential primaries. The order formed part of the resolution of the state’s lawsuit against the Trump Foundation and its directors.

Trump admitted personally misusing Foundation funds. The admissions included allowing his campaign to control the timing, amounts and recipients of approximately $2.8 million raised through a January 2016 veterans fundraiser. He also admitted using charitable money to settle obligations of companies he controlled and purchasing a $10,000 portrait with Foundation funds.

The Foundation had agreed to dissolve under court supervision in December 2018. The resolution directed its remaining $1.78 million in assets and Trump’s damages payment to eight independent charities. It required training for the Trump children and imposed restrictions on Trump’s future charitable service, including independent oversight and a five-year reporting requirement if he formed a new charity.

supported_facts: November 7, 2019 AG announcement confirms $2 million damages order, admissions of Foundation misuse, court-supervised December 2018 dissolution, and future charitable-service restrictions.
January 2016 fundraiser was campaign-controlled; Foundation grants approximately $2.8 million.
Five-year requirement concerns reporting if Trump creates a new charity, not a five-year ban on heading charities.

terminal.title: Trump’s Hurricane Maria Response in Puerto Rico: Visit, Relief Challenges and Later Mortality Estimate
terminal.description_short: Trump’s October 2017 Puerto Rico visit after Hurricane Maria included a paper-towel distribution at a relief center.
terminal.description_medium: After Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017, Trump visited on October 3 and tossed paper towels to residents. He had authorized a Jones Act shipping waiver on September 28. GAO later found staffing, logistics and infrastructure failures slowed FEMA’s response. An August 2018 George Washington University report estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 through February 2018.
terminal.description_long: Donald Trump visited Puerto Rico on October 3, 2017, after Hurricane Maria devastated the island in September. Reuters photographed him tossing rolls of paper towels into a crowd of residents affected by the storm at a chapel in San Juan. The visit followed his September 28 authorization of a Jones Act waiver intended to expedite relief supplies. ABC News reported criticism of the pace of aid and of the administration’s earlier failure to waive the shipping restrictions. A September 2018 Government Accountability Office report documented challenges that slowed and complicated FEMA’s response. Successive hurricanes created staffing shortages; the territories’ distance from the mainland complicated deployment of personnel and supplies; and damaged power, communications and local response systems required FEMA to assume duties ordinarily performed by territorial authorities. Separately, George Washington University researchers published a report in August 2018 estimating 2,975 excess deaths associated with Maria between September 2017 and February 2018. Their statistical analysis compared observed mortality with an expected baseline, adjusting for age, sex and migration. The estimate describes deaths associated with the hurricane and its aftermath; it does not assign those deaths to Trump’s visit or quantify the contribution of particular federal decisions.

proposal.description_long: Hurricane Maria made landfall in Puerto Rico in September 2017 and caused widespread damage to infrastructure, housing and communications. President Donald Trump visited the island on October 3. During a stop at a relief center, he tossed rolls of paper towels to people gathered there, an action that attracted criticism and became a prominent image of the visit. The federal response faced documented operational problems. The Government Accountability Office later reported that sequential disasters created staffing shortages, logistical challenges impeded the rapid deployment of personnel and supplies, and damage to local systems required FEMA to assume functions normally handled by territorial authorities. Separately, a George Washington University study estimated 2,975 excess deaths associated with Hurricane Maria through August 2018; GAO described that figure as Puerto Rico’s then-current official count. “Excess deaths” compares observed deaths with an expected baseline and should not be conflated with a count of deaths individually certified as directly caused by the storm. These sources support the visit, the distribution scene, response challenges and the later mortality estimate. They do not establish that the paper-towel event caused FEMA delays, nor do they provide support for every claim about the Jones Act or funding transfers in the original description. The title is narrowed to the documented visit; the response and mortality context is stated with attribution.
proposal.description_medium: Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in September 2017. Trump visited on October 3 and tossed paper towels to people at a relief center. GAO later found that staffing, logistics and infrastructure problems complicated FEMA’s response. A George Washington University study estimated 2,975 excess deaths through August 2018; this is an excess-mortality estimate, not a count of deaths individually attributed to the storm. The evidence does not connect the paper-towel scene to response delays.

raw_line: {"record_id": "entry-5698", "status": "pass", "title": "NARA Sought Untransferred Trump Presidential Records; 15 Boxes Returned in 2022", "description_short": "NARA said it worked with Trump representatives in 2021 to locate records not transferred at term’s end; 15 boxes were transported in January 2022.", "description_medium": "NARA said it worked with Trump representatives in 2021 to locate presidential records not transferred when his administration ended. A representative reported finding some records in December. NARA arranged secure transport and received 15 boxes from Mar-a-Lago in mid-January 2022. Representatives told the agency that they were continuing to search for additional presidential records.", "description_long": "During 2021, the National Archives and Records Administration worked with Donald Trump’s representatives to locate presidential records that had not been transferred when his administration ended. In statements issued on February 7 and 8, 2022, NARA explained the sequence leading to the return of 15 boxes from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property in Florida. A representative informed the agency in December 2021 that some records had been located. NARA then arranged secure transport to Washington, receiving the boxes in mid-January 2022. Trump’s representatives also told NARA that they were continuing to search for additional presidential records belonging to the Archives. terminal.title: NARA Sought Untransferred Trump Presidential Records; 15 Boxes Returned in 2022
terminal.description_short: NARA said it worked with Trump representatives in 2021 to locate records not transferred at term’s end; 15 boxes were transported in January 2022.
terminal.description_medium: NARA said it worked with Trump representatives in 2021 to locate presidential records not transferred when his administration ended. A representative reported finding some records in December. NARA arranged secure transport and received 15 boxes from Mar-a-Lago in mid-January 2022. Representatives told the agency that they were continuing to search for additional presidential records.
terminal.description_long: During 2021, the National Archives and Records Administration worked with Donald Trump’s representatives to locate presidential records that had not been transferred when his administration ended. In statements issued on February 7 and 8, 2022, NARA explained the sequence leading to the return of 15 boxes from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property in Florida. A representative informed the agency in December 2021 that some records had been located. NARA then arranged secure transport to Washington, receiving the boxes in mid-January 2022. Trump’s representatives also told NARA that they were continuing to search for additional presidential records belonging to the Archives. The agency said these records should have been transferred from the White House at the end of Trump’s administration in January 2021 under the Presidential Records Act. Archivist David Ferriero emphasized that complete presidential records enable public accountability and that NARA pursues records improperly removed or not appropriately transferred. NARA said its officials had not visited or raided Mar-a-Lago to collect these boxes.

terminal.description_medium: NARA said it worked with Trump representatives in 2021 to locate presidential records not transferred when his administration ended. A representative reported finding some records in December. NARA arranged secure transport and received 15 boxes from Mar-a-Lago in mid-January 2022. Representatives told the agency that they were continuing to search for additional presidential records.
terminal.description_long: During 2021, the National Archives and Records Administration worked with Donald Trump’s representatives to locate presidential records that had not been transferred when his administration ended. In statements issued on February 7 and 8, 2022, NARA explained the sequence leading to the return of 15 boxes from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property in Florida. A representative informed the agency in December 2021 that some records had been located. NARA then arranged secure transport to Washington, receiving the boxes in mid-January 2022. Trump’s representatives also told NARA that they were continuing to search for additional presidential records belonging to the Archives. The agency said these records should have been transferred from the White House at the end of Trump’s administration in January 2021 under the Presidential Records Act. Archivist David Ferriero emphasized that complete presidential records enable public accountability and that NARA pursues records improperly removed or not appropriately transferred. NARA said its officials had not visited or raided Mar-a-Lago to collect these boxes.

 Feb 09, 2026 3:09 PM 

 

 Photo illustration by Slate. Photo by Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images. 

Pete Hegseth, perhaps the most thuggish, toadying, all-around underqualified secretary of defense in the job’s nearly 80-year history, has now shown himself to be the most institutionally destructive as well.

His announcement on Friday, that he was cutting the department’s ties to Harvard University—and possibly to other centers of higher learning too—reflects not only a smug anti-intellectualism, which is out of sync with a high-tech modern military, but also a total misunderstanding of how and why its ties to academia first came about.

“For too long,” Hegseth said in a video, “this department has sent our best and brightest officers to Harvard, hoping the university would better understand and appreciate our warrior class. Instead, too many of our officers came back looking too much like Harvard—heads full of globalist and radical ideologies that do not improve our fighting ranks. … We train warriors, not wokesters. Harvard, good riddance.”

From start to finish, this speech is pure rubbish.

The need to broaden the education of America’s warriors was first perceived by Gen. George Marshall, the U.S. Army’s chief of staff during World War II (hardly an emblem of woke). Marshall relied heavily on the chief of his Strategy and Policy Group, Brig. Gen. George Lincoln. (I delved into his papers at the West Point Archives for Chapter 1 of my 2013 book The Insurgents: David Petraeus and the Plot to Change the American Way of War.)

In the last year of the war—at age 37 the Army’s youngest general officer—Lincoln met with Marshall daily, coordinated every major military campaign, and helped draft the treaties at Yalta and Potsdam, which shaped the political map of postwar Europe. He then assisted Marshall’s replacement, Gen. Dwight Eisenhower, in creating the Department of Defense.

The special thing about Lincoln was, after graduating from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 1929, he won a Rhodes scholarship and spent the next three years at Oxford, studying philosophy, politics, and economics—then returned to West Point to teach before getting assigned to high-level staff jobs after WWII broke out.

While working with Marshall at the various Allied planning conferences, Lincoln noticed that much of the crucial work was done by a handful of fellow military officers, almost all of whom had also been Rhodes scholars. He did a little research and found that West Point had produced 13 Rhodes scholars in its history. Of the six still alive, four were holding senior policy posts, helping set the terms of military strategy and postwar peace treaties.

As the war ended, the United States was emerging as a global power with global responsibilities. It would need leaders well versed in politics, diplomacy, economics, and strategy. But few such people existed in or out of the military. Certainly West Point, Lincoln’s alma mater, wasn’t training such people. At the time, all its cadets took the same courses, which focused mainly on engineering. There was a course on bridge building, but no courses on military history.

In May 1945, less than two weeks after the end of the war, Lincoln wrote a letter to one of his mentors back at West Point. “I am beginning to think that what we need is a type of staff officer with at least three heads—one political, one economic, and one military.” In another letter, he proposed “baptizing practically all officers” with a “sprinkling” of education in politics, history, and economics, while taking “certain selected” officers and “dunking” them in those waters much more deeply.

The Army, he continued, “can no longer afford to depend on the fortuitous assembly of Rhodes Scholars. … There must be an integrated system of high-level training if Army policy and national policy are properly to be served, a system which begins here at West Point.”

Lincoln could easily have gone on to have a storied career, rising through the Army’s officer corps. Instead, he returned to West Point to create a new department of social sciences, which would mold this new system. Since regulations required that department heads be colonels, not generals, Lincoln even took a demotion in his rank and was never again promoted.

He started his new job on Sept. 1, 1947. He and Col. Herman Beukema, his onetime mentor and now the new department’s co-founder, created courses in history, government, foreign affairs, geography, national-security economics, and international relations. Lincoln also wrote the nation’s first college-level textbook on international politics, a reference that was assigned not only at West Point but at several civilian colleges across the country.

Over time, cadets concentrating in social sciences formed an elite enclave, which became an object of resentment and ridicule among some more hidebound officers. As late as 1991, when Gen. “Stormin’ Norman” Schwarzkopf returned from his command of Operation Desert Storm to deliver a rousing victory speech at West Point, he reminisced about his own days as a cadet and poked fun at the crazy ideas advanced by “a couple of left-wing pinko Social Science instructors.”

Schwarzkopf was mining a well-known stereotype. (Even at this late date, some of the cadets laughed at and applauded his remark.) He was only half joking, however. Some of his own staff officers had been products of “Sosh,” the academy’s nickname for the social sciences department. But Schwarzkopf’s jab (minus the humor) is the view that Hegseth now holds of the entire enterprise: seeing war as nothing more than killing. In this view, all other dimensions of warfare—the idea that soldiers should understand the enemy they’re fighting, interpret their tactics in a strategic context, and stay within the confines of international law—are not merely secondary but counterproductive, contrary to a “warrior spirit,” woke.

Lincoln had another purpose in creating the new department. “I am certain,” he wrote in one letter, “that we must make strenuous efforts … to improve the so-called Army mind.” This would mean, above all, “impressing the student with the fact that the basic requirement is to learn to think—sometimes a very painful process.”

Perhaps more than anything else, this is what Hegseth sees, and fears, in the officers who have earned degrees or fellowships at places like Harvard. This spirit of inquiry, curiosity, and criticism is what he defines as “woke.”

Lincoln died in 1975, but the Sosh tradition lived on. Today almost all general officers in the U.S. Army (and also in the Air Force, which was a branch of the Army until 1947, when it became an independent service) hold graduate degrees—and most of them, at least the generals I know, are as proud of their degrees as they are of their ranks.

For instance, Gen. David Petraeus, commander of the more successful phases of the war in Iraq, went to West Point, then earned a Ph.D. at Princeton University. Gen. H.R. McMaster, who was a lethal tank commander and a counterinsurgency strategist in Iraq (as well as, briefly, national security adviser during Donald Trump’s first term as president), followed a similar path, getting his Ph.D. from the University of North Carolina.

Maybe Hegseth sees those officers as epitomes of woke. But what about the current chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Gen. Dan Caine, appointed and lauded by Trump and his entire team, including Hegseth? His page on the JCS website states that Caine “has completed a range of national security and leadership courses, including Harvard Kennedy School’s course for Senior Executives in National and International Security.”

Someone should ask Caine, the next time he appears at a press conference or a congressional hearing, whether his spirit and skill as a warrior and a citizen were helped or hindered by his Ivy League exposure. Maybe Hegseth should have asked the question—and maybe he should think and read up even a little bit about a vast range of topics before opening his mouth.

Peter Brian Hegseth (born June 6, 1980) is an American government official, veteran, and former television personality who has been serving as the 29th United States secretary of defense since 2025.

Hegseth studied politics at Princeton University, where he was the publisher of The Princeton Tory, a conservative student newspaper. In 2003, he was commissioned as an infantry officer in the Minnesota Army National Guard, serving at Guantanamo Bay Naval Base and deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan. Hegseth worked for several organizations after leaving Iraq, including as an executive director at Vets For Freedom and Concerned Veterans for America. He became a contributor to Fox News in 2014. Hegseth served as an advisor to President Donald Trump after supporting his campaign in 2016. From 2017 to 2024, Hegseth co-hosted Fox & Friends Weekend. He has written several books, including American Crusade (2020) and The War on Warriors (2024).

In November 2024, then-President-elect Trump named Hegseth as his nominee for secretary of defense. In a Senate Committee on Armed Services hearing days before Trump's second inauguration, Hegseth faced allegations of sexual misconduct, financial mismanagement, and excessive drinking. Hegseth was confirmed by the Senate that month, with the vice president, JD Vance, casting a tie-breaking vote. It was only the second time in U.S. history that a Cabinet nominee's confirmation was decided by a vice president, following Betsy DeVos during the first Trump administration in 2017. Hegseth is the second-youngest secretary of defense after Donald Rumsfeld, who first occupied the position in the Ford administration.

Hegseth has drawn criticism during his tenure as secretary of defense for a variety of actions such as the fallout from a leaked government group chat on Signal; alleged war crimes related to U.S. military strikes on alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean Sea; promoting Christianity inside the military; using unmarked military planes for boat strikes; the use of force and rules of engagement in the 2026 Iran war; and a military mandate for testosterone screening. ## Early life and education

Princeton University, where Hegseth studied (pictured in 2019)

Peter Brian Hegseth was born on June 6, 1980, in Minneapolis, Minnesota. [13] He is of Norwegian descent, as his great-grandparents migrated from Norway to Minnesota before they had children. [14] He was the first of three children of Brian Hegseth and Penelope Haugen. [15] [16] [b] Hegseth's father was a basketball coach for high schools across Minnesota before retiring in 2019. [16] Hegseth's mother is an executive business coach [18] who has taught with the Minnesota Excellence in Public Service (MEPS) Series, a fellowship and leadership program for Republican and center-right women. [15] Hegseth was raised in Forest Lake, Minnesota, [19] and attended Forest Lake Area High School. [20] He graduated on June 10, 1999 as valedictorian. Hegseth played on his high school's football team and was a point guard on the basketball team, where he set school records for career three-point shots, single-season three-point shots, and single-season three-point shooting percentage. He was named all-conference twice and earned all-state honors as a senior. [21] 

After high school, Hegseth enrolled at Princeton University, [22] where he graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in politics in 2003. [22] [23] According to Reserve & National Guard Magazine, he chose Princeton over an offer from the United States Military Academy to play for the school's basketball team. [24] Months before the September 11 attacks, Hegseth joined the Reserve Officers' Training Corps. [25] During his years at Princeton, Hegseth [21] was the publisher and editor-in-chief of The Princeton Tory, the school's conservative student newspaper. [26] 

In April 2002, Hegseth declared that, as publisher of The Princeton Tory, he would "defend the pillars of Western civilization against the distractions of diversity". [27] The editors of The Princeton Tory criticized Halle Berry for accepting the Academy Award for Best Actress for her performance in Monster's Ball (2001) "on behalf of an entire race", and The New York Times for announcing that it would print gay marriage announcements, arguing that it would justify publishing marriage announcements for incestuous, zoophilic, and pedophilic relationships. [28] In October, The Princeton Tory published an editorial calling homosexuality immoral. In response, the president of Princeton's student government, Nina Langsam, wrote a strongly worded email to Hegseth and The Princeton Tory' s publisher, Brad Simmons. Her email was published in the following issue. [29] [30] 

### Military service (2003–2006, 2010–2014, 2019–2021)

Hegseth meeting with Mahmood Kalaf Ahmed, the mayor of Samarra, in 2005

After graduating from Princeton in 2003, Hegseth was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the United States Army through the university's Reserve Officers' Training Corps program. [19] [31] He briefly worked as an equity-markets analyst at Bear Stearns. [26] Hegseth completed his basic training at Fort Benning in Columbus, Georgia, in 2004, [24] and for 11 months he was a Minnesota Army National Guardsman at Guantanamo Bay detention camp. [31] There, he led a platoon of soldiers from the New Jersey Army National Guard [25] guarding detainees. [26] By July 2005, he had returned to Bear Stearns; [31] shortly thereafter, he volunteered in the Iraq War as an infantry officer, [24] where he received a Bronze Star Medal. [26] Hegseth served in the 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry Regiment [25] in the 101st Airborne Division, led by Colonel Michael D. Steele. [32] He began his tour in Baghdad before moving to Samarra, [19] where he served as a civil affairs officer, [33] working with the city council and forming an alliance with council member Asaad Ali Yaseen. [19] Hegseth has described a near-death experience in Iraq in which a rocket-propelled grenade hit his vehicle but failed to detonate. [34] 

In 2010, Hegseth deployed with the Minnesota Army National Guard as a counterinsurgency instructor. [19] He volunteered to teach at the Counterinsurgency Training Center in Kabul, Afghanistan, for eight months, [19] during the withdrawal of United States troops from Afghanistan; [32] he taught one of the final classes at the school. [25] After completing his tour in 2014, he was promoted to major [26] and assigned to the Individual Ready Reserve. [24] Through the reserve, he joined the District of Columbia Army National Guard in June 2019 as a traditional drilling service member, remaining in duty until March 2021. [35] He was barred from serving on duty at the inauguration of Joe Biden after a guardsman flagged Hegseth as an "insider threat", noting a tattoo on his biceps of the words Deus vult. [36] He left the Individual Ready Reserve in January 2024, writing in his book The War on Warriors (2024) that he resigned over the incident. [37] 

### Political activism (2006–2016)

Hegseth speaking at the Defend Freedom Tour in 2013

By August 2006, [25] Hegseth moved to Manhattan and began working at the Manhattan Institute for Policy Research, [19] where he met a marine who was working for Vets for Freedom, a political advocacy organization. [26] He began working for Vets for Freedom in 2006 as an unpaid director; [38] by 2007, he was working full-time as an executive director, [39] and by 2008, he became the organization's president. [38] In May 2007, Hegseth appeared at a presidential campaign fundraiser for John McCain. [42] By January 2009, Vets for Freedom had accrued hundreds of thousands of dollars in unpaid bills, leading to an internal campaign to oust Hegseth. After returning to Minnesota in February 2012, [19] Hegseth decided to enter the Republican primary for the United States Senate election in Minnesota and had selected a campaign manager, Anne Neu Brindley. [46] He founded MN PAC to support similar candidates, though a third of the organization's funds went to parties for personal friends and family. [26] Hegseth began working as president of Concerned Veterans of America, a group funded by the Koch brothers, [47] that year. [48] The group criticized President Obama for the 2014 Veterans Health Administration controversy. [26] In December, President-elect Donald Trump considered Hegseth for secretary of veterans affairs, but he faced opposition from veterans groups who viewed Hegseth's support for allowing all veterans to choose private doctors as untenable; Paul Rieckhoff, the executive director of Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America, said that selecting Hegseth would "be war" and "a radical departure" for the department. # Hegseth is purging military leaders with little explanation 

 Nov. 7, 2025 at 5:36 pm Updated Nov. 7, 2025 at 6:36 pm 

By 

Eric Schmitt

Helene Cooper

WASHINGTON — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired or sidelined at least two dozen generals and admirals over the past nine months in a series of ousters that could reshape the U.S. military for years to come.

His actions, which are without precedent in recent decades, have come with little explanation. In many cases, they have run counter to the advice of top military leaders who fought alongside the officers in combat, senior military officials said. 

The utter unpredictability of Hegseth’s moves, as described in interviews with 20 current and former military officials, has created an atmosphere of anxiety and mistrust that has forced senior officers to take sides and, at times, pitted them against one another. 

Hegseth has delayed or canceled the promotions of at least four senior military officers because they previously worked for Gen. Mark Milley, a former chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff whom President Donald Trump loathes and has repeatedly accused of disloyalty. One is Maj. Gen. James Patrick Work, who was expected to be the deputy commander at U.S. Central Command, which oversees troops in the Middle East, officials said. 

Work, one of the Army’s most combat-experienced officers, played a crucial role leading U.S. and Iraqi troops to victory over the Islamic State group in Mosul, Iraq, during the first Trump administration. He also served as Milley’s executive officer in 2018, which might have led Hegseth to view him with skepticism, senior Army officials said. 

Despite the strong backing of top Army leaders, Work remains in limbo, his future uncertain, senior military officials said.

Other officers fell out of favor after being targeted on social media by right-wing influencers or because they had voiced support years earlier for diversity, equity and inclusion programs. Rear Adm. Milton Sands, the commander of the Navy SEALs, who pushed to have female instructors in SEAL training, was fired by Hegseth in August. 

Some leaders were ousted for offering candid military assessments. Hegseth soured on Adm. Alvin Holsey, the head of U.S. Southern Command, after he raised questions about deadly military strikes on boats in the Caribbean Sea. The Trump administration has said, without offering detailed evidence, that the boats were trafficking drugs. Holsey abruptly announced last month that he was stepping down, less than one year into what is typically a three-year assignment. 

Another senior officer, Lt. Gen. Jeffrey A. Kruse, a 35-year Air Force intelligence officer who led the Defense Intelligence Agency, was forced from his position after his agency cast doubt on Trump’s assertion that U.S. airstrikes in June had “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear program. 

In his public appearances, Hegseth has stressed “unity” as a critical component of a lethal military. “Your strength is your shared purpose,” he told several hundred troops recently on a trip to Asia. “Your strength is the unity of our mission.” 

But his actions have worked to undermine that critical asset, military officials said.

Hegseth, a former Fox News commentator and Army National Guard major, began his tenure by firing several high-profile military leaders, including Gen. CQ Brown Jr., the chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Since then, the defense secretary has targeted an array of officers who seemed destined to ascend to four-star rank. 

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s top spokesperson, said in a statement that the “military has never been more unified” and cited Hegseth’s work to dismantle the Biden administration’s diversity, equity and inclusion agenda and restore the military’s “warrior ethos.” 

“The department will continue to elevate those in our ranks who are committed to warfighting and meritocracy,” the statement read.

A new administration has the right to choose military leaders it trusts, said Kori Schake, a defense specialist who served on the National Security Council in the administration of President George W. Bush. But she worried the Trump administration was “squandering an enormous amount of talent.” 

The scale of the firings also has alarmed some in Congress, like Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who previously served as a CIA officer analyzing foreign militaries. She recently described Hegseth’s moves as a “purge.”

“The places where we’ve looked at these kinds of things are places like China,” she said. “I used to work on Iraq. They would do the same thing.”

Another concern: Hegseth’s moves have fed the impression that there are pro-Trump and anti-Trump generals, officials said.

In a September speech attended by hundreds of senior officers from around the world, Hegseth singled out several recently retired four-star generals for scorn.

“The new compass heading is clear,” Hegseth told the officers gathered at Quantico, Va. “Out with the Chiarellis, the McKenzies and the Milleys.” He was referring to Gen. Peter W. Chiarelli, the former Army vice chief of staff, and Gen. Kenneth F. McKenzie Jr., a former head of Central Command.

Several officers in the crowd that day had worked for the generals Hegseth disparaged and considered them mentors. So, too, had more junior officers.

“The message being sent to those younger soldiers and sailors and airmen and Marines is that politics can and should be part of your military service,” said Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a former Army Ranger. “It’s a dangerous message.”

Hegseth’s personnel moves have hit several of the Army’s most admired and combat-tested leaders. In late October, he forced Lt. Gen. J.P. McGee from his position as the director of strategy and war plans on the Joint Staff, military officials said. The move was reported earlier by CNN. 

McGee deployed 10 times to war zones, according to his military records. Work, who stepped down in August as the commander of the 82nd Airborne Division, spent nearly six years in combat zones over the course of his career.

## Sponsored

Military officials spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal personnel matters at a time when the Pentagon’s culture has become increasingly punitive.

Until recently, Work’s promotion seemed like a certainty. All 10 of the officers who commanded the 82nd Airborne before him were promoted to three-star rank. Nine made four-stars. It is still possible that Work will fight through Hegseth’s doubts and earn a third star, senior Army officials said. 

Most of the officers forced out by Hegseth are likely to land on their feet, hired by defense contractors, big companies or universities. The biggest blow may be felt by those left behind.

Many of Hegseth’s dismissals have left senior military leaders and even Trump administration officials puzzled and speculating about the cause.

Such was the case with Gen. James J. Mingus, the Army’s vice chief of staff. Senior Army officials assumed that Mingus would stay in his position until at least next summer. The four-star officer has played a critical role, alongside Gen. Randy George, the Army’s chief of staff, in remaking the Army for high-intensity combat and drone warfare in the Pacific. 

Instead, his retirement was hastily announced Oct. 21 with little input from senior Army leaders or Army Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll, military officials said. No reason was given for Mingus’ early dismissal or his replacement by Lt. Gen. Christopher C. LaNeve, who formerly led the 82nd Airborne Division. 

In the case of Rear Adm. Michael Donnelly, the end came because of a 7-year-old story, recycled through the right-wing media. The Pentagon announced in June that Donnelly, the former commander of the aircraft carrier Ronald Reagan, was being nominated to be vice admiral and commander of the Navy’s largest overseas force, the 7th Fleet. 

But in July, Hegseth withdrew the nomination after The Daily Wire reported that Donnelly had allowed drag performances on the aircraft carrier.

Navy officials said the article belied what had actually happened: One sailor in drag performed during a talent show on the carrier. Donnelly was in Singapore at the time.

As of the end of October, the Navy was still on the hunt for a new 7th Fleet commander.

Some rising stars have survived right-wing scrutiny. Lt. Gen. Jonathan P. Braga, a decorated Special Operations officer, was sharply criticized in a conservative blog for promoting diversity initiatives. But the strong backing of several senior officers in the elite Special Operations community, which Hegseth respects, protected him. Braga took over the shadowy Joint Special Operations Command, which includes the Army’s Delta Force and the Navy’s SEAL Team 6, in late September. 

In late September, Lt. Gen. Douglas A. Sims II’s 34-year military career came to an abrupt end at a military base near the Pentagon.

On the day of his retirement, Sims marched past columns of soldiers in their dress uniforms who were awaiting his review. The Army band played a John Philip Sousa march. A row of howitzers sounded a thundering 17-gun salute.

Sims had been the Army’s choice to run Forces Command, a four-star job focused on making sure that commanders around the world have trained-and-ready forces available to them. The command, while important, is rarely a source of controversy, and the choice of who will lead it is usually left to the Army. 

But Hegseth blocked Sims’ promotion because he was seen as too close to Milley, according to three people with knowledge of the matter.

Before he officially departed the Army, Sims recited the names of the five soldiers killed under his command. His last remarks in uniform focused on the values that hold an Army together through hard times — the same values many senior military officials worried were now under strain. 

“Everything we do is about people,” Sims reminded the crowd. “The military doesn’t have a monopoly in this regard, but the stakes of what we do are just different.”

Gen. Dan Caine, the chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, listened in the packed bleachers next to Brown, his predecessor, whom Hegseth had fired in February.

Photo by Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images. \n\nPete Hegseth, perhaps the most thuggish, toadying, all-around underqualified secretary of defense in the job’s nearly 80-year history, has now shown himself to be the most institutionally destructive as well.\n\nHis announcement on Friday, that he was cutting the department’s ties to Harvard University—and possibly to other centers of higher learning too—reflects not only a smug anti-intellectualism, which is out of sync with a high-tech modern military, but also a total misunderstanding of how and why its ties to academia first came about.\n\n“For too long,” Hegseth said in a video, “this department has sent our best and brightest officers to Harvard, hoping the university would better understand and appreciate our warrior class. Instead, too many of our officers came back looking too much like Harvard—heads full of globalist and radical ideologies that do not improve our fighting ranks. … We train warriors, not wokesters. Harvard, good riddance.”\n\nFrom start to finish, this speech is pure rubbish.\n\nThe need to broaden the education of America’s warriors was first perceived by Gen. George Marshall, the U.S. Army’s chief of staff during World War II (hardly an emblem of woke). Marshall relied heavily on the chief of his Strategy and Policy Group, Brig. Gen. George Lincoln. (I delved into his papers at the West Point Archives for Chapter 1 of my 2013 book The Insurgents: David Petraeus and the Plot to Change the American Way of War.)\n\nIn the last year of the war—at age 37 the Army’s youngest general officer—Lincoln met with Marshall daily, coordinated every major military campaign, and helped draft the treaties at Yalta and Potsdam, which shaped the political map of postwar Europe. He then assisted Marshall’s replacement, Gen. Dwight Eisenhower, in creating the Department of Defense.\n\nThe special thing about Lincoln was, after graduating from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 1929, he won a Rhodes scholarship and spent the next three years at Oxford, studying philosophy, politics, and economics—then returned to West Point to teach before getting assigned to high-level staff jobs after WWII broke out.\n\nWhile working with Marshall at the various Allied planning conferences, Lincoln noticed that much of the crucial work was done by a handful of fellow military officers, almost all of whom had also been Rhodes scholars. He did a little research and found that West Point had produced 13 Rhodes scholars in its history. Of the six still alive, four were holding senior policy posts, helping set the terms of military strategy and postwar peace treaties.\n\nAs the war ended, the United States was emerging as a global power with global responsibilities. It would need leaders well versed in politics, diplomacy, economics, and strategy. But few such people existed in or out of the military. Certainly West Point, Lincoln’s alma mater, wasn’t training such people. At the time, all its cadets took the same courses, which focused mainly on engineering. There was a course on bridge building, but no courses on military history.\n\nIn May 1945, less than two weeks after the end of the war, Lincoln wrote a letter to one of his mentors back at West Point. “I am beginning to think that what we need is a type of staff officer with at least three heads—one political, one economic, and one military.” In another letter, he proposed “baptizing practically all officers” with a “sprinkling” of education in politics, history, and economics, while taking “certain selected” officers and “dunking” them in those waters much more deeply.\n\nThe Army, he continued, “can no longer afford to depend on the fortuitous assembly of Rhodes Scholars. … There must be an integrated system of high-level training if Army policy and national policy are properly to be served, a system which begins here at West Point.”\n\nLincoln could easily have gone on to have a storied career, rising through the Army’s officer corps. Instead, he returned to West Point to create a new department of social sciences, which would mold this new system. Since regulations required that department heads be colonels, not generals, Lincoln even took a demotion in his rank and was never again promoted.\n\nHe started his new job on Sept. 1, 1947. He and Col. Herman Beukema, his onetime mentor and now the new department’s co-founder, created courses in history, government, foreign affairs, geography, national-security economics, and international relations. Lincoln also wrote the nation’s first college-level textbook on international politics, a reference that was assigned not only at West Point but at several civilian colleges across the country.\n\nOver time, cadets concentrating in social sciences formed an elite enclave, which became an object of resentment and ridicule among some more hidebound officers. As late as 1991, when Gen. “Stormin’ Norman” Schwarzkopf returned from his command of Operation Desert Storm to deliver a rousing victory speech at West Point, he reminisced about his own days as a cadet and poked fun at the crazy ideas advanced by “a couple of left-wing pinko Social Science instructors.”\n\nSchwarzkopf was mining a well-known stereotype. (Even at this late date, some of the cadets laughed at and applauded his remark.) He was only half joking, however. Some of his own staff officers had been products of “Sosh,” the academy’s nickname for the social sciences department. But Schwarzkopf’s jab (minus the humor) is the view that Hegseth now holds of the entire enterprise: seeing war as nothing more than killing. In this view, all other dimensions of warfare—the idea that soldiers should understand the enemy they’re fighting, interpret their tactics in a strategic context, and stay within the confines of international law—are not merely secondary but counterproductive, contrary to a “warrior spirit,” woke.\n\nLincoln had another purpose in creating the new department. “I am certain,” he wrote in one letter, “that we must make strenuous efforts … to improve the so-called Army mind.” This would mean, above all, “impressing the student with the fact that the basic requirement is to learn to think—sometimes a very painful process.”\n\nPerhaps more than anything else, this is what Hegseth sees, and fears, in the officers who have earned degrees or fellowships at places like Harvard. This spirit of inquiry, curiosity, and criticism is what he defines as “woke.”\n\nLincoln died in 1975, but the Sosh tradition lived on. Today almost all general officers in the U.S. Army (and also in the Air Force, which was a branch of the Army until 1947, when it became an independent service) hold graduate degrees—and most of them, at least the generals I know, are as proud of their degrees as they are of their ranks.\n\nFor instance, Gen. David Petraeus, commander of the more successful phases of the war in Iraq, went to West Point, then earned a Ph.D. at Princeton University. Gen. H.R. McMaster, who was a lethal tank commander and a counterinsurgency strategist in Iraq (as well as, briefly, national security adviser during Donald Trump’s first term as president), followed a similar path, getting his Ph.D. from the University of North Carolina.\n\nMaybe Hegseth sees those officers as epitomes of woke. But what about the current chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Gen. Dan Caine, appointed and lauded by Trump and his entire team, including Hegseth? His page on the JCS website states that Caine “has completed a range of national security and leadership courses, including Harvard Kennedy School’s course for Senior Executives in National and International Security.”\n\nSomeone should ask Caine, the next time he appears at a press conference or a congressional hearing, whether his spirit and skill as a warrior and a citizen were helped or hindered by his Ivy League exposure. Maybe Hegseth should have asked the question—and maybe he should think and read up even a little bit about a vast range of topics before opening his mouth.\n\n# Pete Hegseth\nURL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Hegseth\n\nPete Hegseth\n\n| Pete Hegseth | |\n| --- | --- |\n| Official portrait, 2025 | |\n| 29th United States Secretary of Defense [a] | |\n| Incumbent | |\n| Assumed office January 25, 2025 | |\n| President | Donald Trump |\n| Deputy | Steve Feinberg |\n| Preceded by | Lloyd Austin |\n| Personal details | |\n| Born | Peter Brian Hegseth June 6, 1980 (age 46) Minneapolis, Minnesota, U.S. |\n| Party | Republican |\n| Spouses | Meredith Schwarz ​ ​(m. 2004; div. 2009)​ Samantha Deering ​ ​(m. 2010; div. 2017)​ Jennifer Rauchet ​(m. 2019)​ |\n| Children | 4 [2] |\n| Education | Princeton University (BA) Harvard University (MPP) |\n| Signature | |\n| Military service | |\n| Branch/service | United States Army Army National Guard |\n| Years of service | 2003–2006 2010–2014 2019–2021 |\n| Rank | Major |\n| Unit | 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry Regiment Minnesota Army National Guard District of Columbia Army National Guard |\n| Battles/wars | Iraq War War in Afghanistan |\n| Awards | Bronze Star (2) Joint Service Commendation Medal Army Commendation Medal (2) Combat Infantryman Badge |\n| Hegseth's voice Hegseth addressing the 2025 United States strikes on Iranian nuclear sites Recorded June 22, 2025 | |\n\nPeter Brian Hegseth (born June 6, 1980) is an American government official, veteran, and former television personality who has been serving as the 29th United States secretary of defense since 2025.\n\nHegseth studied politics at Princeton University, where he was the publisher of The Princeton Tory, a conservative student newspaper. In 2003, he was commissioned as an infantry officer in the Minnesota Army National Guard, serving at Guantanamo Bay Naval Base and deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan. Hegseth worked for several organizations after leaving Iraq, including as an executive director at Vets For Freedom and Concerned Veterans for America. He became a contributor to Fox News in 2014. Hegseth served as an advisor to President Donald Trump after supporting his campaign in 2016. From 2017 to 2024, Hegseth co-hosted Fox & Friends Weekend. He has written several books, including American Crusade (2020) and The War on Warriors (2024).\n\nIn November 2024, then-President-elect Trump named Hegseth as his nominee for secretary of defense. In a Senate Committee on Armed Services hearing days before Trump's second inauguration, Hegseth faced allegations of sexual misconduct, financial mismanagement, and excessive drinking. Hegseth was confirmed by the Senate that month, with the vice president, JD Vance, casting a tie-breaking vote. It was only the second time in U.S. history that a Cabinet nominee's confirmation was decided by a vice president, following Betsy DeVos during the first Trump administration in 2017. Hegseth is the second-youngest secretary of defense after Donald Rumsfeld, who first occupied the position in the Ford administration.\n\nHegseth has drawn criticism during his tenure as secretary of defense for a variety of actions such as the fallout from a leaked government group chat on Signal; alleged war crimes related to U.S. military strikes on alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean Sea; promoting Christianity inside the military; using unmarked military planes for boat strikes; the use of force and rules of engagement in the 2026 Iran war; and a military mandate for testosterone screening. [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9] Conversely, Hegseth has received praise from Republican politicians, right-wing political commentators, and Christian nationalist organizations for his role as defense secretary. [10] [11] [12] \n\n## Early life and education\n\nPrinceton University, where Hegseth studied (pictured in 2019)\n\nPeter Brian Hegseth was born on June 6, 1980, in Minneapolis, Minnesota. [13] He is of Norwegian descent, as his great-grandparents migrated from Norway to Minnesota before they had children. [14] He was the first of three children of Brian Hegseth and Penelope Haugen. [15] [16] [b] Hegseth's father was a basketball coach for high schools across Minnesota before retiring in 2019. [16] Hegseth's mother is an executive business coach [18] who has taught with the Minnesota Excellence in Public Service (MEPS) Series, a fellowship and leadership program for Republican and center-right women. [15] Hegseth was raised in Forest Lake, Minnesota, [19] and attended Forest Lake Area High School. [20] He graduated on June 10, 1999 as valedictorian. Hegseth played on his high school's football team and was a point guard on the basketball team, where he set school records for career three-point shots, single-season three-point shots, and single-season three-point shooting percentage. He was named all-conference twice and earned all-state honors as a senior. [21] \n\nAfter high school, Hegseth enrolled at Princeton University, [22] where he graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in politics in 2003. [22] [23] According to Reserve & National Guard Magazine, he chose Princeton over an offer from the United States Military Academy to play for the school's basketball team. [24] Months before the September 11 attacks, Hegseth joined the Reserve Officers' Training Corps. [25] During his years at Princeton, Hegseth [21] was the publisher and editor-in-chief of The Princeton Tory, the school's conservative student newspaper. [26] \n\nIn April 2002, Hegseth declared that, as publisher of The Princeton Tory, he would \"defend the pillars of Western civilization against the distractions of diversity\". [27] The editors of The Princeton Tory criticized Halle Berry for accepting the Academy Award for Best Actress for her performance in Monster's Ball (2001) \"on behalf of an entire race\", and The New York Times for announcing that it would print gay marriage announcements, arguing that it would justify publishing marriage announcements for incestuous, zoophilic, and pedophilic relationships. [28] In October, The Princeton Tory published an editorial calling homosexuality immoral. In response, the president of Princeton's student government, Nina Langsam, wrote a strongly worded email to Hegseth and The Princeton Tory' s publisher, Brad Simmons. Her email was published in the following issue. [29] [30] \n\n### Military service (2003–2006, 2010–2014, 2019–2021)\n\nHegseth meeting with Mahmood Kalaf Ahmed, the mayor of Samarra, in 2005\n\nAfter graduating from Princeton in 2003, Hegseth was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the United States Army through the university's Reserve Officers' Training Corps program. [19] [31] He briefly worked as an equity-markets analyst at Bear Stearns. [26] Hegseth completed his basic training at Fort Benning in Columbus, Georgia, in 2004, [24] and for 11 months he was a Minnesota Army National Guardsman at Guantanamo Bay detention camp. [31] There, he led a platoon of soldiers from the New Jersey Army National Guard [25] guarding detainees. [26] By July 2005, he had returned to Bear Stearns; [31] shortly thereafter, he volunteered in the Iraq War as an infantry officer, [24] where he received a Bronze Star Medal. [26] Hegseth served in the 3rd Battalion, 187th Infantry Regiment [25] in the 101st Airborne Division, led by Colonel Michael D. Steele. [32] He began his tour in Baghdad before moving to Samarra, [19] where he served as a civil affairs officer, [33] working with the city council and forming an alliance with council member Asaad Ali Yaseen. [19] Hegseth has described a near-death experience in Iraq in which a rocket-propelled grenade hit his vehicle but failed to detonate. [34] \n\nIn 2010, Hegseth deployed with the Minnesota Army National Guard as a counterinsurgency instructor. [19] He volunteered to teach at the Counterinsurgency Training Center in Kabul, Afghanistan, for eight months, [19] during the withdrawal of United States troops from Afghanistan; [32] he taught one of the final classes at the school. [25] After completing his tour in 2014, he was promoted to major [26] and assigned to the Individual Ready Reserve. [24] Through the reserve, he joined the District of Columbia Army National Guard in June 2019 as a traditional drilling service member, remaining in duty until March 2021. [35] He was barred from serving on duty at the inauguration of Joe Biden after a guardsman flagged Hegseth as an \"insider threat\", noting a tattoo on his biceps of the words Deus vult. [36] He left the Individual Ready Reserve in January 2024, writing in his book The War on Warriors (2024) that he resigned over the incident. [37] \n\n### Political activism (2006–2016)\n\nHegseth speaking at the Defend Freedom Tour in 2013\n\nBy August 2006, [25] Hegseth moved to Manhattan and began working at the Manhattan Institute for Policy Research, [19] where he met a marine who was working for Vets for Freedom, a political advocacy organization. [26] He began working for Vets for Freedom in 2006 as an unpaid director; [38] by 2007, he was working full-time as an executive director, [39] and by 2008, he became the organization's president. [38] In May 2007, Hegseth appeared at a presidential campaign fundraiser for John McCain. [40] In the months leading up to the 2008 United States presidential election, Vets for Freedom began supporting McCain. [41] As the group's chairman, he criticized Democratic nominee Barack Obama for supporting \"a dangerous policy of irreversible withdrawal.\" [42] By January 2009, Vets for Freedom had accrued hundreds of thousands of dollars in unpaid bills, leading to an internal campaign to oust Hegseth. The group merged with Military Families United, and he was removed from leadership by 2011. [26] \n\nAfter returning to Minnesota in February 2012, [19] Hegseth decided to enter the Republican primary for the United States Senate election in Minnesota and had selected a campaign manager, Anne Neu Brindley. [43] By April, his campaign had raised US$160,000. [44] Hegseth lost to Kurt Bills in the Republican convention in May, [45] and ended his candidacy days later. [46] He founded MN PAC to support similar candidates, though a third of the organization's funds went to parties for personal friends and family. [26] Hegseth began working as president of Concerned Veterans of America, a group funded by the Koch brothers, [47] that year. [48] The group criticized President Obama for the 2014 Veterans Health Administration controversy. [49] Hegseth enrolled in the Harvard Kennedy School in 2009, but completed just one semester; [19] he graduated in 2013 with a degree in public policy. [21] In 2022, [50] to protest the offering of classes in critical race theory at Harvard University, he reportedly wrote \"Return to sender\" on his degree [51] and sent it back to the university. [52] \n\nHegseth left Concerned Veterans for America in January 2016 [53] after allegations of financial mismanagement and alcoholism. A whistleblower report accused Hegseth of fostering a sexist and hostile workplace at Concerned Veterans for America; one whistleblower claimed that Hegseth had used organization funds as a personal expense account. Another former employee claimed he had witnessed Hegseth drunkenly chanting \"Kill all Muslims!\" [26] In December, President-elect Donald Trump considered Hegseth for secretary of veterans affairs, but he faced opposition from veterans groups who viewed Hegseth's support for allowing all veterans to choose private doctors as untenable; Paul Rieckhoff, the executive director of Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America, said that selecting Hegseth would \"be war\" and \"a radical departure\" for the department. [53] Trump later chose David Shulkin, with The Washington Post noting Hegseth's lack of experience in operating a large organization. [54] Hegseth told podcaster Shawn Ryan that Trump found him too young to assume the position. [55] After Shulkin fell out of favor with the Trump administration in March 2018, Hegseth positioned himself as a potential candidate, [56] but Trump selected Robert Wilkie after consulting Hegseth and financier Isaac Perlmutter. [57] \n\n### Fox News (2014–2024)\n\nHegseth interviewing Secretary of State Mike Pompeo on Fox & Friends in March 2020\n\nBy June 2014, Hegseth was given a position as a regular contributor to Fox News [58] by the network's executive, Roger Ailes. [59] In 2016, he was briefly a host on TheBlaze [60] before regularly hosting Fox & Friends Weekend that year after Ailes's resignation, becoming an official co-host in January 2017. [59] According to a Fox News executive in Hoax (2020), Jennifer Rauchet, a producer of Fox & Friends Weekend who later married him, \"was favoring Pete with airtime\" and \"kept putting Pete on TV.\" [61] Hegseth served as a temporary host for Laura Ingraham on The Ingraham Angle in an effort by the network to promote other staffers; the change occurred during the boycott of The Ingraham Angle after comments Ingraham made about David Hogg, an activist and survivor of the Parkland high school shooting. [62] He hosted All-American New Year (2018) with commentator Lisa Kennedy. [63] \n\nHegseth's opinions expressed on Fox & Friends influenced Trump's policymaking in his first term. In October 2018, as a migrant caravan began traveling to the United States, Trump claimed that \"unknown Middle Easterners\" had infiltrated the caravan. Trump apparently cited a comment that Hegseth had made on Fox & Friends, though Hegseth said he had not verified his statement's accuracy. [64] Hegseth had apparently based his claim on a statement Guatemalan president Jimmy Morales made after capturing 100 ISIS fighters in the country. [65] In negotiations to avert a federal government shutdown, Democrats neared a deal until Hegseth urged Trump not to support a deal that did not include US$5 billion for his border wall. [66] Trump repeated claims Hegseth had made correlating video games with mass shootings after two mass shootings in El Paso and in Dayton in August 2019. [67] Hegseth said he had spoken to Trump about pardoning war criminal Clint Lorance and accused murderer Mathew L. Golsteyn, as well as reversing the demotion of Eddie Gallagher. [68] \n\nAt Fox News, Hegseth was the subject of multiple lawsuits. In 2015, he threw an axe during a Flag Day event in New York City, accidentally hitting a drummer from the United States Military Academy. Video of the incident circulated widely online. The drummer, Jeff Prosperie, alleged that he had suffered \"severe and serious personal injuries to his mind and body\" and \"permanent effects of pain, disability, disfigurement and loss of body function.\" Prosperie sued Hegseth three years later in 2018, [69] and the suit was resolved in 2019. [70] In Dominion Voting Systems v. Fox News Network (2023), Dominion Voting Systems included a segment of Fox & Friends Weekend featuring Hegseth with co-hosts Will Cain and Rachel Campos-Duffy, in which they did not reject claims by Rudy Giuliani that the company's voting machines facilitated voting fraud in the 2020 presidential election. [71] \n\nHegseth was chosen among Fox News's hosts to be featured on Fox Nation, the network's streaming service. [72] To promote the service, he co-hosted a one-hour special, Fox Nation First Look, with Jesse Watters, Tomi Lahren, Britt McHenry, and Tyrus. [73] On Fox Nation, Hegseth hosted The Miseducation of America (2022–2023), a television program criticizing \"the Left's educational agenda\". [74] He also hosted the series Battle in the Holy Land (2019–2023), [75] The Life of Jesus (2022–2023), and the special Battle in Bethlehem (2019), on the service. [31] \n\n## Secretary of Defense (2025–present)\n\n### Nomination and confirmation\n\nHegseth testifying at his confirmation hearing before the Senate Committee on Armed Services on January 14, 2025\n\nOn November 12, 2024, President-elect Donald Trump named Hegseth as his nominee for secretary of defense, [76] after Arkansas senator Tom Cotton announced he would not serve as secretary. [77] Hegseth subsequently ended his contract with Fox News. [50] The selection of Hegseth was seen as a sign that Trump sought to appoint a loyalist to lead the Department of Defense, [c] and his relative lack of experience surprised officials in the department. [d] According to Vanity Fair, Trump's transition team became aware the following day of a sexual assault allegation involving Hegseth that occurred in Monterey, California, seven years prior; [84] The Washington Post reported that senior officials on the team were surprised by the allegation and reconsidered his nomination. [85] Despite the allegation, Trump defended Hegseth [86] and several Republican senators indicated that they would support him. [87] His nomination was threatened by an article from Jane Mayer in The New Yorker detailing alleged financial mismanagement and alcohol issues while leading his veterans' groups, [26] while an NBC News article reported that his drinking habits concerned his colleagues at Fox News; [88] The New York Times reported in December that Trump had begun to consider Florida governor Ron DeSantis as an alternative. [89] \n\nIn an effort to retain his nomination amid controversies, Hegseth began a campaign that month. Advisors to Trump privately sought to persuade him to support Hegseth in fear that it would embolden recalcitrant Republican senators, while he could not garner support for DeSantis, according to The New York Times. In addition, the Times reported that Vice President-elect JD Vance had led a group of Republicans, including Donald Trump Jr., former Trump aide Steve Bannon, political activist Charlie Kirk, and Breitbart News reporter Matt Boyle, to support Hegseth's nomination. [90] Trump allies took a direct approach to addressing the controversies, including an interview with Megyn Kelly that impressed Trump. (AP Photo/Gail Burton)\n\nCOLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — The Trump administration’s attempts to obtain state-level voter data have suffered yet another legal blow.\n\nU.S. District Court Judge Stephanie Gallagher last week dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit against Maryland that sought access to the state’s voter records.\n\nGallagher, appointed by Republican President Donald Trump during his first term, wrote that she “joins every court to have addressed this issue” in concluding that the unredacted voter registration file “is not a record or paper that a state must produce to the United States.”\n\nWith the dismissal Thursday in Maryland, the number of states where the Justice Department has lost similar cases comes to nine. # Pete Hegseth is taking the U.S. military backward.

Published: 2026-02-09
Author: Fred Kaplan
